cases.hpi: {{patient_name}} presents to the emergency department with acute onset chest pain and severe respiratory distress. The patient appears diaphoretic, tachypneic, and in extremis. cases.hpi: {{patient_name}} is an elderly patient with a history of chronic alcoholism who presents to the emergency department with altered mental status following a recent fall. The patient has had episodic confusion and fluctuating consciousness since the fall. The subdural hematoma risk is elevated due to advanced age and chronic alcohol use, both of which contribute to brain atrophy and increased tension on bridging veins. Time is critical — expanding hematoma may cause mass effect and progressive neurological deterioration.

physical_exam: Fluctuating level of consciousness. Assess for lateralizing signs, pupil asymmetry, and GCS. Focal deficits may indicate mass effect from expanding hematoma.

cases.hpi: {{patient_name}} is a reproductive-age woman who presents with severe pelvic pain that worsens with sexual activity. The pain is localized to the right adnexal region. Differential for a right adnexal mass in a reproductive-age female is broad and includes ectopic pregnancy, tuboovarian abscess, inflammatory bowel disease, ovarian mass, endometrioma, theca lutein cysts, and germ cell neoplasms. Imaging and appropriate surgical consultation are required.

rationale.Physical Exam: General Appearance: The general examination is extremely useful to determine how sick the patient looks.
rationale.Physical Exam: Chest / Lungs: Patient in moderate distress — important to look for pulmonary problems.
rationale.Physical Exam: Heart / Cardiovascular: Patient in moderate distress — important to look for cardiovascular problems.
rationale.Physical Exam: Abdomen: This is the presenting chief complaint — abdominal exam is required.
rationale.Physical Exam: Genitalia: Pelvic pain can present as abdominal pain — should be examined.
rationale.Physical Exam: HEENT / Neck: Will show dry mucous membranes — key finding in DKA.
rationale.Physical Exam: Skin: Will show low skin turgor from dehydration.
rationale.HCG, beta, urine/serum qualitative: Every female patient of childbearing age should have a pregnancy test done.
rationale.Hemoglobin A1C, blood: Expected to be elevated with new-onset diabetes. Not required for acute management.
rationale.Arterial blood gases: ABGs are not required in DKA. Bicarbonate levels and anion gap are sufficient to monitor correction. Best way to monitor DKA resolution is disappearance of elevated anion gap.
rationale.Urinalysis: Important to see extent of chronic diabetes. Patient spilling protein into urine with normal creatinine.
rationale.CBC with differential: Important to rule out infection. Leukocyte count is high — DKA patients often have elevated counts from catecholamine release and dehydration.
rationale.Basic metabolic profile / Comprehensive: Will find extremely high blood glucose. Important to monitor electrolytes — DKA can cause pseudohypercalcemia.
rationale.Insulin (regular / lispro / glargine / N: Mainstay treatment for DKA is insulin. Patient will slowly improve once insulin treatment initiated.
rationale.Normal saline / Lactated Ringer / 0.45%: IV fluids should be given to every DKA patient. Normal saline or LR if sodium is normal.
rationale.Potassium replacement (KCl / K citrate /: Potassium must be checked prior to insulin therapy — insulin worsens pre-existing hypokalemia, risking fatal cardiac arrhythmias. Start replacement if K < 5.3. KCl is preferred as patients are chloride-depleted.
rationale.Intravenous access: Good practice to order IV access when administering IV fluids/medications.
rationale.Dextrose solutions: Patient is already hyperglycemic in the 600s — additional glucose is not warranted. Glucose can be added once levels reach 250 range, but should not be used during initial treatment.
rationale.Papanicolaou smear / HPV DNA test: Patient has not had a recent pap smear — this should be done.
rationale.Tdap vaccine: Tdap should be given every 10 years. No history given — should be administered.
rationale.HPV vaccine: HPV vaccine should be given to females ages 11-26.
rationale.Advise patient, no illegal drug use: If patient admits to illicit drug use, it is important to advise against use.
rationale.Instruct patient, diabetes: Patient needs diabetes education about proper glucose management after discharge.
rationale.CT abdomen/pelvis with contrast: While abdominal pain warrants investigation, markedly elevated glucose (600s) with anion gap acidosis is diagnostic of DKA. Treat the DKA first — the pain resolves with insulin and fluids.
rationale.Broad-spectrum antibiotics: Leukocytosis in DKA is caused by catecholamine release and dehydration, not infection. No evidence of infectious source.
rationale.Surgical consult for acute abdomen: Abdominal pain in DKA can mimic acute abdomen but resolves with metabolic correction. Surgery is not indicated.
rationale.Dextrose-containing fluids initially: Patient has glucose in the 600s. Dextrose would worsen hyperglycemia. Only add dextrose once glucose reaches ~250 mg/dL.

cases.hpi: {{patient_name}} is a 22-year-old woman with no known past medical history who presents to the emergency department with diffuse abdominal pain, lethargy, and vomiting for two days. She reports increased appetite prior to symptom onset, along with blurry vision, dizziness, drowsiness, and polyuria. She is on oral contraceptives and has a family history of diabetes in a sibling. Exam reveals dry mucous membranes, decreased skin turgor, and tachycardia. Point-of-care glucose is markedly elevated in the 600s. The clinical picture is consistent with new-onset diabetic ketoacidosis — the abdominal pain is a common presenting feature of DKA, not a primary surgical abdomen.

correct_orders: Basic metabolic profile / Comprehensive metabolic profile / Liver function panel

rationale.Physical Exam: General Appearance: The general examination is extremely useful to determine how sick the patient looks.
rationale.Physical Exam: Chest / Lungs: Important to look for lung pathology in a febrile patient.
rationale.Physical Exam: Abdomen: Important to look for abdominal pathology in a febrile patient.
rationale.Physical Exam: Neuro / Psych: This is the patient's chief complaint — neurologic exam is essential.
rationale.Physical Exam: Skin: This will reveal pink macular lesions on the left thigh — characteristic rash.
rationale.CBC with differential: Important to order a CBC with differential in a patient with fever.
rationale.Chest X-ray: Important to get a chest X-ray to rule out pneumonia and other causes of fever.
rationale.Urinalysis: Important to get urinalysis to rule out bacterial infection and other causes of fever.
rationale.Toxicology screen, urine: Urine tox screen is important as illicit drugs can cause fever.
rationale.Bacterial culture, blood: Blood culture will aid in localizing the source of infection.
rationale.MRI/CT head: Ataxia should lead to consideration of neurological infection or stroke. Brain imaging to rule out stroke or tumor. MRI preferred (more sensitive for West Nile abnormalities) but CT acceptable.
rationale.Lumbar puncture: Lumbar puncture is essential for evaluation of patient with ataxia and fever.
rationale.Protein, cerebrospinal fluid: CSF analysis is important in patient with fever and neurological signs.
rationale.Fungal culture, cerebrospinal fluid: Important to culture CSF for viral, bacterial, and fungal etiologies.
rationale.Viral culture, cerebrospinal fluid: Important to culture CSF. Note: West Nile virus is frequently negative in viral culture.
rationale.Bacterial culture, cerebrospinal fluid: Important to culture CSF for bacterial etiologies.
rationale.Glucose, cerebrospinal fluid: CSF glucose points toward fungal, viral, or bacterial picture. Normal glucose suggests viral (not bacterial) etiology.
rationale.Cell count, cerebrospinal fluid: CSF cell count consistent with aseptic meningitis. Lymphocytic predominance suggests viral etiology.
rationale.West Nile virus antibody, CSF/serum: Confirms aseptic meningitis is from West Nile virus.
rationale.HSV PCR, CSF/serum: Aseptic meningitis workup should include herpes simplex screening.
rationale.Basic metabolic profile / Comprehensive: Chemistries are an important screening tool and should be done in nearly every non-emergent patient.
rationale.Tdap vaccine: Tdap should be given every 10 years. No history given — should be administered.
rationale.Papanicolaou smear: HPV DNA test every 3 years for women ≥30 with normal cytology. No history given — should be scheduled.
rationale.Mammography: USPSTF recommends mammogram screening every 2 years for patients ages 50-69.
rationale.Empiric antibiotics without LP: Bacterial meningitis is on the differential and requires CSF culture before antibiotics. But this is viral encephalitis — LP is diagnostic, not empiric.
rationale.Corticosteroids: No evidence for steroids in West Nile encephalitis. Supportive care is the mainstay.
rationale.Discharge from office: Patient with encephalitis requires inpatient monitoring. West Nile can progress to flaccid paralysis and respiratory failure.

cases.hpi: {{patient_name}} is a 55-year-old woman who presents with fever, headache, and progressive ataxia. She has developed pink macular lesions on the left thigh. Neurological examination reveals cerebellar signs. The combination of fever, neurological symptoms, and characteristic rash in the appropriate season raises concern for arboviral encephalitis. West Nile virus is the leading consideration among mosquito-borne neuroinvasive diseases. Diagnostic workup must include brain imaging to rule out stroke or mass lesion, followed by lumbar puncture for CSF analysis.

West Nile virus is the leading consideration among mosquito-borne neuroinvasive diseases. Diagnostic workup must include brain imaging to rule out stroke or mass lesion, followed by lumbar puncture for CSF analysis.
physical_exam: Ataxia — cerebellar findings. Fever with neurological signs = CNS infection until proven otherwise. Assess for nuchal rigidity, photophobia, focal deficits.

cases.hpi: {{patient_name}} is a 6-year-old child who presents with fever, sore throat, malaise, and generalized rash. Exam reveals posterior cervical lymphadenopathy, palatal petechiae, and splenomegaly. The combination of pharyngitis, lymphadenopathy, fever, and the characteristic maculopapular rash is classic for infectious mononucleosis caused by Epstein-Barr virus. The differential includes other viral infections (CMV, acute HIV), streptococcal pharyngitis, and toxoplasmosis. Key management considerations: avoid amoxicillin/ampicillin (causes characteristic EBV rash), avoid aspirin (Reye syndrome risk in febrile children), and in older patients, restrict contact sports to prevent splenic rupture.

rationale.Physical Exam: General Appearance: Determine how sick the patient looks.
rationale.Physical Exam: Chest / Lungs: Investigate for lung pathology — respiratory muscle weakness can cause hypoventilation.
rationale.Physical Exam: Genitalia: Pelvic pain can present as abdominal pain — should be examined.

rationale.CT chest with contrast / MRI chest: CT chest is essential to rule out thymoma, seen in 10-15% of MG patients. Thymoma appears as anterior mediastinal mass.
rationale.CBC with differential: Good screening tool in nearly every patient.
rationale.ECG, 12 lead: Generalized weakness can be cardiac. ECG rules out cardiac etiologies.

rationale.Acetylcholine receptor antibody, serum: Positive detection strongly supports MG diagnosis. ~80% positive in generalized MG.
rationale.Electromyography: EMG with repetitive stimulation shows decremental response — decreased signal with each stimulation. Differentiates from Lambert-Eaton (which shows incremental response).
rationale.Tensilon test: Not required but would be positive in MG. Edrophonium temporarily improves muscle strength.
rationale.PT/PTT / INR: Patient is likely to have surgery (thymectomy) — pre-surgical labs needed.
rationale.Basic metabolic profile / Comprehensive: BMPs are excellent screening tools in any differential.
rationale.Methylprednisolone / Prednisone / Azathi: Corticosteroids and azathioprine are first-line immunosuppressive treatments for MG.
rationale.Pyridostigmine / Neostigmine: Pyridostigmine is for symptomatic treatment only — acetylcholinesterase inhibitor that increases ACh at neuromuscular junction. Does NOT treat underlying disease. Use in conjunction with immunosuppressants.
rationale.Consult surgery / Thymectomy: Thymoma should be surgically removed. Thymectomy can lead to complete remission in ~85% of patients without further medication.
rationale.IVIG / Plasmapheresis: Can be used pre-thymectomy for severe symptoms. However, expensive — conservative trial of steroids + pyridostigmine first is reasonable if patient is stable.
rationale.Instruct patient, smoking cessation: One of the most important things for health — address smoking.
rationale.Advise patient, safe sex techniques: Patient has history of STIs — review safe sex practices.
rationale.Reassure patient: New chronic diagnosis causes anxiety — reassure and inform.
rationale.Papanicolaou smear: HPV DNA test every 3 years for women ≥30. No history given — should be scheduled.
rationale.Tdap vaccine: Tdap every 10 years. No history given — should be administered.
rationale.Intubation / mechanical ventilation (too: Patient has respiratory muscle weakness but intubation is invasive and can often be avoided with medical management of MG first.
rationale.Pyridostigmine as monotherapy: Pyridostigmine only treats symptoms. In a patient with respiratory involvement, immunosuppression (steroids/azathioprine) is needed to treat the underlying autoimmune process. Pyridostigmine also increases airway secretions.

cases.hpi: {{patient_name}} is a woman of childbearing age who presents with progressive generalized weakness that worsens with continued muscle use and improves with rest. She has developed ptosis, dysarthria, and dysphagia. Respiratory muscle involvement is present with mild hypoxemia from hypoventilation. Exam reveals fatigable weakness with preservation of sensation and reflexes — the hallmark of myasthenia gravis. cases.hpi: {{patient_name}} is a 19-year-old sexually active man who presents with dysuria, fevers, and chills. Rectal exam reveals an edematous, tender prostate — the key finding that localizes the infection to the prostate rather than the bladder or urethra alone. rationale.Physical Exam: General Appearance: Determine how sick the patient looks.

rationale.ECG, 12 lead: Rule out cardiac causes of leg pain. PAD patients often have concomitant CAD.
rationale.Hemoglobin A1C, blood: All patients with possible PVD should be evaluated for diabetes.
rationale.Lipid profile: Lipids contribute to atherosclerosis — check and treat if abnormal. Goal LDL < 100 in PAD.

rationale.Angiography, lower extremity: Invasive test with contrast risks. Conservative management first for intermittent claudication, not rest pain.
rationale.Metformin: First-line therapy for type 2 diabetes. Start at diagnosis.
rationale.ACE inhibitor (Lisinopril / Enalapril /: ACE inhibitors are first-line for hypertensive diabetics — nephroprotective. ARB if ACEI intolerant.
rationale.Statin (Atorvastatin / Rosuvastatin / Si: Statin for hyperlipidemia — prevents worsening of PVD. Goal LDL < 100 mg/dL.
rationale.Aspirin, therapy: Antiplatelet therapy indicated for PAD. Aspirin is most common and most tested. Reduces cardiovascular events.
rationale.Instruct patient, smoking cessation: One of the most important interventions — smoking accelerates PVD.
rationale.Diet modification (calorie-restricted /: Weight loss to control diabetes and hypertension. DASH diet for hypertension.
rationale.Instruct patient, diabetes: Diabetes education increases compliance and improves outcomes.
rationale.Advise patient, exercise program: Exercise is excellent for weight loss, glucose control, and collateral circulation development. Supervised walking programs improve claudication symptoms.
rationale.Angiography / Arteriography: Invasive, uses contrast (nephrotoxic, allergic reactions), expensive. Conservative management with risk factor modification is first-line for intermittent claudication. Only for rest pain or failed medical therapy.
rationale.Surgical bypass / Angioplasty: Not indicated for intermittent claudication. Reserved for rest pain, tissue loss, or disabling symptoms refractory to conservative therapy.
rationale.CT angiography: Radiation + iodinated contrast exposure. Duplex ultrasound or ABI is preferred non-invasive screening.

cases.hpi: {{patient_name}} is a middle-aged man with multiple cardiovascular risk factors — hypertension, hyperlipidemia, newly diagnosed type 2 diabetes, and smoking — who presents with bilateral leg pain on exertion that is relieved by rest (intermittent claudication). He has diminished peripheral pulses and cool extremities. The ankle-brachial index is less than 0.7, consistent with moderate PAD (normal ≥ 1.0, claudication < 0.7, rest pain < 0.4). Importantly, he has intermittent claudication rather than rest pain, which means conservative management is appropriate rather than invasive intervention. The 6 P's of peripheral artery disease are: Pulselessness, Pain, Pallor, Poikilothermia, Paresthesia, and Paralysis.

cases.hpi: {{patient_name}} is a man who recently returned from a cruise ship and presents with abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, jaundice, and shortness of breath. He has RUQ tenderness on exam. LFTs are markedly elevated in the 2000-3000 range. The cruise ship travel and profoundly elevated transaminases are highly suspicious for acute viral hepatitis A (fecal-oral transmission). Management is supportive: IV fluids, antiemetics, oxygen for hypoxia, and antibiotics for aspiration pneumonia per ATS/IDSA guidelines (treat as community-acquired pneumonia; no anaerobic coverage needed without abscess/empyema). Acetaminophen is contraindicated with hepatic injury. Admit to inpatient unit.

cases.hpi: {{patient_name}} is a sexually active young adult who presents with dysuria, purulent urethral discharge, and scrotal swelling. The patient admits to illicit drug use and risky sexual practices. Chlamydia trachomatis is the most common bacterial STI — an obligate intracellular pathogen. Co-infection with gonorrhea is common (40% of women, 20% of men), so empiric treatment for both is recommended even if only chlamydia is confirmed. Most cases are asymptomatic (80% women, 50% men), making the presence of overt urethritis clinically useful. First-line diagnosis is NAAT (DNA probe) on first-catch urine. cases.hpi: {{patient_name}} is an older man with chronic osteoarthritis who presents with epigastric abdominal pain of one week's duration. History reveals extensive, prolonged use of oral ibuprofen for knee pain. NSAIDs block both COX-1 and COX-2, impairing gastric prostaglandin production and disrupting mucosal defense — this is classic NSAID-induced gastropathy. Symptoms began one week ago and the patient is medically stable. Conservative management is key: discontinue NSAIDs, start a proton-pump inhibitor, and follow up in 2-4 weeks. If no improvement with conservative therapy, then EGD would be indicated, but ordering it now loses points — the USMLE tests restraint from invasive testing. H. pylori should be ruled out. For his osteoarthritis, switch to acetaminophen and/or topical diclofenac gel rather than oral NSAIDs. Address modifiable risk factors: smoking cessation and alcohol avoidance.

cases.hpi: {{patient_name}} is a pregnant woman at 33 weeks gestation who presents with facial and upper extremity edema, severe hypertension (189/99), new-onset headaches, and blurry vision — signs of end-organ damage. Pre-eclampsia is defined as SBP > 140 or DBP > 90 developing after 20 weeks gestation WITH end-organ dysfunction (proteinuria, visual/cerebral disturbances, pulmonary edema, creatinine > 1.1, elevated LFTs, or thrombocytopenia < 100,000). With SBP > 160, she meets criteria for pre-eclampsia with severe features. Management triad: (1) Magnesium sulfate for seizure prophylaxis to prevent progression to eclampsia, (2) IV labetalol or hydralazine for blood pressure control (labetalol is superior with fewer side effects), (3) Betamethasone for fetal lung maturity if delivering < 34 weeks. Definitive treatment is delivery — with severe features, deliver at ≥ 34 weeks. OB/GYN consult for cesarean section. Admit to ICU or inpatient unit — this is an emergency.

rationale.ECG, 12 lead: ECG on every chest pain patient. Will show diffuse ST elevation in pericarditis (not territorial like MI).

rationale.Echocardiography (transthoracic): TTE shows small pericardial effusion. Transthoracic is sufficient — TEE is unnecessary and invasive.
rationale.Chest X-ray: Rule out other causes of chest pain.
rationale.ANA, serum: Autoimmune etiology is one cause of pericarditis.
rationale.Echocardiography, transesophageal: TTE is more than sufficient. TEE is invasive and unnecessary for small pericardial effusion — points lost for ordering.
rationale.NSAIDs (Ibuprofen / Naproxen / Aspirin): NSAIDs are treatment of choice for acute pericarditis.
rationale.Colchicine: Added to NSAID therapy — reduces symptoms AND decreases rate of recurrent pericarditis. Well tolerated. Should be added for first-episode acute pericarditis.
rationale.PPI / H2 blocker (Omeprazole / Famotidin: High-dose NSAID therapy requires GI protection with PPI or H2 blocker.
rationale.Pericardiocentesis: Only small effusion — will resolve on its own. Pericardiocentesis only for moderate/large effusions (>2 cm) or tamponade.
rationale.Advise patient, rest at home: Activity may trigger recurrence. Rest until symptoms resolve.
rationale.Transesophageal echocardiography: Invasive and unnecessary. TTE is sufficient to evaluate pericardial effusion. Ordering TEE loses points.
rationale.NSAIDs alone (without colchicine): Colchicine should be added to NSAID therapy for first-episode acute pericarditis — it reduces recurrence rate and improves symptom resolution.
rationale.Glucocorticoids as first-line: Steroids are reserved for refractory pericarditis unresponsive to NSAIDs/colchicine, or autoimmune-associated pericarditis.

cases.hpi: {{patient_name}} is a man with no significant past medical history who presents with acute chest pain that is pleuritic (worse with inspiration) and positional (relieved by leaning forward). He has no history of recent viral infection, making this likely idiopathic pericarditis. ECG shows diffuse ST elevation. Echocardiogram reveals a small pericardial effusion — no tamponade physiology. Troponin is negative, ruling out MI. First-line treatment: NSAIDs (ibuprofen/naproxen) PLUS colchicine — colchicine reduces symptoms and decreases rate of recurrent pericarditis. Add a PPI/H2 blocker for GI protection with high-dose NSAID therapy. Rest until symptoms resolve — activity can trigger recurrence. Pericardiocentesis is NOT indicated for small, asymptomatic effusions (only for moderate/large effusions > 2 cm or tamponade). Transesophageal echo is unnecessary — transthoracic echo is sufficient.

cases.hpi: {{patient_name}} presents with painless cervical lymphadenopathy and constitutional B-symptoms (weight loss, night sweats, fever). Hodgkin's lymphoma is a B-cell malignancy defined by Reed-Sternberg cells — 'owl-eyed' nucleoli with clear cytoplasm, CD15+ and CD30+. Excisional lymph node biopsy (NOT FNA) is required for diagnosis to preserve architecture for immunophenotyping and cytogenetics. CXR is initial screening. PET/CT for staging: Stage I (single node), II (≥2 nodes same side of diaphragm), III (both sides), IV (extranodal). Treatment: ABVD chemotherapy (Adriamycin, Bleomycin, Vinblastine, Dacarbazine) ± radiation for early stage. Check albumin as prognostic indicator. Screen for HIV and EBV, which can mimic lymphoma.

cases.hpi: {{patient_name}} presents with constipation, malaise, nausea, and vomiting. Occult blood is positive. Colon cancer is the third most common cancer and third most common cause of cancer mortality in the US. Left colon masses present with obstructive symptoms (constipation, decreased stool caliber); right colon masses present with iron deficiency anemia from occult bleeding. Workup: colonoscopy with biopsy for diagnosis (NOT just flexible sigmoidoscopy — must examine entire colon). CT chest/abdomen/pelvis with contrast for staging (gold standard for metastasis screening). CEA level pre-op for prognosis and recurrence monitoring. Pre-op clearance: ECG, PT/PTT, type and screen, NPO. Treatment: surgical resection (colectomy) by colorectal surgery. If lymph node positive → adjuvant chemotherapy. Follow-up: CEA q3-6mo, CT annually x 5yr, colonoscopy at 1yr then q3yr.

cases.hpi: {{patient_name}} presents with the classic triad of diverticulitis: LLQ pain, low-grade fever, and leukocytosis. He has changes in bowel habits with nausea and vomiting. He meets SIRS criteria (fever >100.4°F, WBC >12,000). CT abdomen/pelvis with IV and oral contrast is the gold standard — findings include bowel wall thickening, pericolic fat stranding, and a 2 cm abscess (complicated diverticulitis). Abscesses <3-4 cm can be managed conservatively with antibiotics alone without percutaneous drainage. Colonoscopy and barium enema are CONTRAINDICATED in acute diverticulitis due to risk of perforation. Treatment: NPO for bowel rest, IV fluids, IV antibiotics (cefazolin + metronidazole, cefuroxime + metronidazole, ceftriaxone + metronidazole, or ampicillin/sulbactam). High-fiber diet at discharge for prevention.

cases.hpi: {{patient_name}} is an older woman with hypertension on hydrochlorothiazide who presents with palpitations, syncope, dizziness, and hypotension. ECG demonstrates complete heart block (3rd degree AV block) — complete dissociation between P waves and QRS complexes with no relationship. This is a bradycardic rhythm. Third-degree AV block has an extensive differential: coronary ischemia (most common), fibrosis/sclerosis of conduction system (Lenegre/Lev disease — likely in this patient given age and HTN), Lyme disease, sarcoidosis, hyperkalemia, thyroid disorders, iatrogenic (AV nodal blockers), and congenital (unlikely — 90% symptomatic by age 30). TSH normal, troponin negative, chemistries normal, ESR normal, CBC normal — infectious and inflammatory causes unlikely. Most likely: fibrous degeneration of conduction system from aging + hypertension. Management: temporary transcutaneous/transvenous pacemaker, then permanent pacemaker placement.

cases.hpi: {{patient_name}} is a 29-year-old who presents with alternating diarrhea and constipation, abdominal pain relieved by defecation, and bloating — meeting Rome IV criteria for IBS (recurrent abdominal pain + ≥2 of: improvement with defecation, change in stool frequency, change in stool appearance). ESR and CRP are normal, ruling out inflammatory bowel disease. Stool studies are negative for infectious etiology. IBS is a diagnosis of exclusion after ruling out celiac disease (anti-tTG, anti-endomysial antibodies), C. difficile, parasites, and colorectal cancer. Conservative management is key: high-fiber diet, lactose-free trial, exercise, trigger food avoidance. Loperamide PRN for diarrhea, antispasmodics (dicyclomine/hyoscyamine) PRN. Colonoscopy/sigmoidoscopy is NOT appropriate — invasive testing loses points in stable patients with normal screening labs. TCA/SSRI for refractory cases at follow-up.

cases.hpi: {{patient_name}} is a young woman found unconscious with respiratory depression, hypotension, and altered mental status. ECG shows widened QRS, prolonged QT — classic TCA cardiotoxicity. The 'Three C's' of TCA poisoning: Coma, Convulsions, Cardiac arrhythmias. Management priorities: ABCs — intubate for airway protection (GCS depressed), mechanical ventilation. IV fluids for hypotension (TCA blocks alpha-1 receptors → vasodilation). Sodium bicarbonate for cardiac toxicity (QRS >100ms or ventricular arrhythmia) — alkalinization to pH 7.45-7.55 favors non-ionized TCA, reducing sodium channel blockade. Activated charcoal via NG tube if within 2 hours of ingestion (airway must be secured first). 'Coma cocktail': check glucose, give thiamine before D50. Naloxone for possible opioid co-ingestion. CT head to rule out trauma (unwitnessed). Aspirin and acetaminophen levels for common co-ingestants. Psychiatry consult after stabilization for suicide attempt.

rationale.Stress test / Stress echo: NO stress tests until patient recovers from acute HF exacerbation.
rationale.Furosemide (Lasix) / Bumetanide / Torsem: Volume overloaded — loop diuretic for rapid symptom improvement.
rationale.Digoxin: Helps symptoms, not outcomes. For moderate-severe CHF (NYHA III-IV) as adjunct.
rationale.Nitroglycerin: Dilates coronary arteries — reduces afterload and improves coronary flow.
rationale.Beta-blocker (Carvedilol / Metoprolol /: Start after diuresis, prior to discharge. Carvedilol preferred (COMET trial: 17% survival benefit over metoprolol). All 3 accepted.
rationale.Stress test during acute exacerbation: Stress tests contraindicated until acute CHF exacerbation resolves. Risk of decompensation.
rationale.Beta-blocker BEFORE diuresis: Beta-blocker should be started after patient is euvolemic (post-diuresis), before discharge. Starting during acute volume overload can worsen hemodynamics.

cases.hpi: {{patient_name}} is an older man with history of prior myocardial infarction and hypertension on lisinopril who presents with progressive dyspnea, orthopnea, PND, and bilateral lower extremity pitting edema. Exam reveals JVD, S3 gallop, pulmonary crackles, and expiratory wheezing. CXR shows pulmonary edema and cardiomegaly. Echo confirms reduced ejection fraction — systolic dysfunction. BNP is elevated. The most common cause of systolic HF is ischemic heart disease. NYHA Class III-IV (symptoms with minimal activity). Treatment: IV loop diuretic (furosemide) for volume overload, continue ACEI, add nitroglycerin for afterload reduction. Once acute exacerbation resolves and patient is euvolemic, start beta-blocker (carvedilol preferred per COMET trial — 17% survival benefit over metoprolol, though bisoprolol and metoprolol succinate also accepted). Digoxin for symptom control if needed. No stress tests until recovered. Admit to inpatient unit. Discharge: low-sodium diet, smoking cessation, alcohol avoidance, pneumococcal and zoster vaccines, Tdap.

cases.hpi: {{patient_name}} is a 6-year-old boy with previously undiagnosed sickle cell disease (HbSS) who presents with generalized body pain, fever, and respiratory distress consistent with acute vaso-occlusive crisis complicated by acute chest syndrome and lobar pneumonia (H. influenzae B). CBC shows anemia. Peripheral smear demonstrates sickled cells. Hemoglobin electrophoresis is REQUIRED for definitive diagnosis — it differentiates HbSS from other thalassemias. Sickle cell disease is autosomal recessive: single amino acid substitution (valine for glutamic acid) on beta-globin chain → HbS. Does not present before 6 months due to protective HbF. Patients are functionally asplenic by age 8 from repeated splenic infarction → susceptible to encapsulated organisms (S. pneumoniae, H. influenzae B, Salmonella). Management: IV fluids (dehydration precipitates sickling), IV opioids (morphine) for severe pain, oxygen for hypoxia, IV ceftriaxone (CAP treatment), blood transfusion if acute chest syndrome with hypoxia unresponsive to O2. Hydroxyurea stimulates HbF production. Penicillin prophylaxis (lifelong if severe infection history). Consult pediatric hematology. Admit to inpatient. Meningococcal vaccine early (asplenia risk).

cases.hpi: {{patient_name}} is a child presenting with chronic cough, recurrent respiratory infections, shortness of breath, and failure to thrive. Exam reveals nasal polyps, clubbing, and diffuse crackles. Cystic fibrosis is an autosomal recessive disorder caused by a mutation in the CFTR gene on chromosome 7. The defect in chloride transport leads to thick, viscous secretions affecting the lungs, pancreas, GI tract, and reproductive system. Diagnosis is made by elevated sweat chloride test (>60 mEq/L). CXR shows hyperinflation and bronchiectasis. Management includes pancreatic enzyme replacement, fat-soluble vitamin supplementation, airway clearance techniques, and aggressive treatment of pulmonary infections.

cases.hpi: {{patient_name}} is a sexually active young woman presenting with bilateral lower abdominal/pelvic pain, cervical motion tenderness, adnexal tenderness, purulent cervical discharge, fever, and leukocytosis. Pelvic inflammatory disease is an ascending infection from the lower genital tract — commonly Chlamydia trachomatis and Neisseria gonorrhoeae, though polymicrobial. Diagnosis is clinical based on CDC criteria: uterine/adnexal tenderness + cervical motion tenderness (minimum). Complications: tubo-ovarian abscess, infertility, ectopic pregnancy, chronic pelvic pain. Treatment: empiric broad-spectrum antibiotics covering chlamydia, gonorrhea, and anaerobes — ceftriaxone 250mg IM once + doxycycline 100mg PO BID x 14 days + metronidazole 500mg PO BID x 14 days. Partner treatment essential. Screen for other STIs. Admit if severe, TOA, pregnant, or failed outpatient treatment.

cases.hpi: {{patient_name}} is a reproductive-age woman presenting with irregular, heavy vaginal bleeding without identifiable structural or systemic cause. This is dysfunctional uterine bleeding (DUB), most commonly anovulatory — unopposed estrogen stimulation leads to endometrial hyperplasia and irregular shedding. cases.hpi: {{patient_name}} is an elderly patient presenting with the classic triad of normal pressure hydrocephalus: (1) gait disturbance ('magnetic gait' — feet feel stuck to floor), (2) urinary incontinence, and (3) progressive cognitive decline/dementia. NPH is one of the few reversible causes of dementia and must be recognized early. CT/MRI shows ventriculomegaly out of proportion to sulcal atrophy, without obstruction. LP opening pressure is NORMAL (<18 cm H2O) — this distinguishes NPH from obstructive hydrocephalus. High-volume LP (30-50 mL CSF removal) with pre- and post- gait assessment is diagnostic: improvement in gait after CSF removal supports the diagnosis and predicts response to VP shunting. Definitive treatment: ventriculoperitoneal shunt.

cases.title: Headache

rationale.Physical Exam: General Appearance: Assess severity — severe headache, distress.
rationale.Physical Exam: Heart / Cardiovascular: Hypertensive emergency → assess for LVH, S4, new murmurs.
rationale.Physical Exam: Neuro / Psych: Headache + visual changes — assess for focal deficits, altered mental status.
rationale.Physical Exam: Fundoscopy: Papilledema, retinal hemorrhages, cotton wool spots, AV nicking — signs of end-organ damage.
rationale.BMP / CMP: Creatinine — assess for acute kidney injury from hypertensive damage.
rationale.CT head without contrast: Rule out intracranial hemorrhage if focal neuro deficits or AMS.
rationale.IV Labetalol / Nicardipine / Clevidipine: IV antihypertensive. Reduce MAP by ≤25% in first hour. Goal DBP 100-105 over 2-6h. Do NOT rapidly normalize BP.
rationale.Admit to ICU: Hypertensive emergency requires ICU for continuous BP monitoring and IV therapy.
rationale.Short-acting nifedipine PO: Rapid, uncontrollable hypotension → cerebral and coronary hypoperfusion → stroke and MI. NEVER use short-acting nifedipine for hypertensive emergency.
rationale.Rapid BP normalization to 120/80: Reduce MAP by ≤25% in first hour. Rapid normalization causes cerebral hypoperfusion (loss of autoregulation). Goal DBP 100-105 over 2-6 hours.

cases.hpi: {{patient_name}} presents with severe headache, blurred vision, and severely elevated blood pressure (>180/120). This is a hypertensive emergency — severe hypertension WITH evidence of acute end-organ damage (headache/visual changes suggesting cerebral involvement, possible papilledema, retinal hemorrhages). Must be distinguished from hypertensive urgency (severe HTN without end-organ damage — manage with oral meds as outpatient). Workup: fundoscopy (papilledema, hemorrhages, exudates), ECG (LVH, ischemia), CXR (pulmonary edema, aortic dissection signs), UA (proteinuria, hematuria), BMP (elevated Cr — renal damage), cardiac enzymes, CT head if focal neuro deficits. Treatment: IV antihypertensives in ICU — reduce MAP by no more than 25% in first hour (too rapid reduction causes cerebral/coronary hypoperfusion). Labetalol IV, nicardipine, or clevidipine. Goal: reduce DBP to 100-105 over 2-6 hours. Do NOT use short-acting nifedipine (risk of rapid uncontrollable hypotension).

cases.hpi: {{patient_name}} presents with new-onset seizure, altered mental status, autonomic hyperactivity (tachycardia, hypertension, diaphoresis, hyperthermia), tremors, and visual/tactile hallucinations (formication). History reveals chronic heavy alcohol use with abrupt cessation 24-72 hours prior. This is alcohol withdrawal progressing to delirium tremens — a medical emergency with 5-15% mortality if untreated. rationale.CT head (if indicated before LP): If papilledema, focal neuro deficit, AMS, seizure, immunocompromised — CT before LP to rule out mass effect.

cases.hpi: {{patient_name}} presents with severe headache, fever, photophobia, nuchal rigidity, and altered mental status. Exam reveals positive Kernig's sign (pain with knee extension when hip flexed 90°) and Brudzinski's sign (involuntary hip/knee flexion with passive neck flexion). Petechial/purpuric rash is present — meningococcemia causes DIC and purpura fulminans. This is a medical emergency. Do NOT delay antibiotics for CT or LP. Blood cultures + LP with CSF analysis (opening pressure, cell count with differential, glucose, protein, Gram stain, culture). CSF: neutrophilic pleocytosis, low glucose (<40 or <2/3 serum), elevated protein, Gram-negative diplococci. Empiric antibiotics: ceftriaxone 2g IV + vancomycin + dexamethasone (before or with first dose). Add ampicillin if Listeria risk (age >50, immunocompromised). Droplet precautions for meningococcal. Chemoprophylaxis for close contacts (rifampin, ciprofloxacin, or ceftriaxone).

cases.hpi: {{patient_name}} presents with painless jaundice, dark urine, clay-colored stools, pruritus, and weight loss — classic for malignant biliary obstruction. Courvoisier's sign: palpable, non-tender gallbladder in a jaundiced patient = malignancy until proven otherwise (most commonly pancreatic head adenocarcinoma). Pancreatic cancer most commonly arises in the head of the pancreas (70%), causing early obstructive jaundice. Late presentation is the rule — most are unresectable at diagnosis. Workup: CT abdomen/pelvis with IV contrast (pancreatic protocol — dual-phase) for staging. CA 19-9 tumor marker (not diagnostic but prognostic and monitors recurrence). ERCP/MRCP for biliary drainage if needed. Biopsy via EUS-FNA. If resectable (localized, no vascular involvement, no mets): pancreaticoduodenectomy (Whipple procedure). If unresectable: palliative biliary stenting, chemotherapy (gemcitabine + nab-paclitaxel or FOLFIRINOX). Poor prognosis — 5-year survival <10%.

cases.title: Epigastric Pain

rationale.Physical Exam: General Appearance: Assess severity — may appear very ill.
rationale.Physical Exam: Abdomen: Epigastric tenderness + guarding. Grey Turner (flank) / Cullen (periumbilical) in severe hemorrhagic pancreatitis.
rationale.BMP / CMP / LFTs: Elevated AST/ALT/ALP/bilirubin if gallstone etiology. Elevated BUN ≥20 at 48h = poor prognosis.
rationale.Lipase: >3x ULN = diagnostic. More sensitive and specific than amylase.
rationale.RUQ ultrasound: Check for gallstones — most common cause.
rationale.CT abdomen/pelvis with IV contrast: At 48-72h if not improving. Assess for necrosis, pseudocyst, abscess.
rationale.IV fluids (Lactated Ringer preferred): Aggressive resuscitation. LR preferred over NS — reduces systemic inflammation. 250-500 mL/hr initially.
rationale.Diet, NPO: Initially NPO for bowel rest. Advance to clear liquids as pain improves.
rationale.IV analgesics (Morphine / Hydromorphone): Pain management. Morphine is acceptable — does NOT worsen pancreatitis (old teaching was incorrect).
rationale.Prophylactic antibiotics in all pancreat: Antibiotics NOT indicated for sterile pancreatic necrosis. Only for confirmed infected necrosis or concurrent infection. Prophylaxis does not improve outcomes.

cases.hpi: {{patient_name}} presents with acute severe epigastric pain radiating to the back, nausea, vomiting, and low-grade fever. Exam reveals epigastric tenderness with guarding, jaundiced sclera, and possibly Grey Turner/Cullen signs in severe cases. Most common causes: gallstones (GET SMASHED mnemonic — Gallstones, Ethanol, Trauma, Steroids, Mumps, Autoimmune, Scorpion stings, Hypercalcemia/Hypertriglyceridemia, ERCP, Drugs). Diagnosis requires 2 of 3: (1) characteristic epigastric pain, (2) lipase/amylase >3x upper limit, (3) CT findings. Lipase is more sensitive and specific than amylase (especially in delayed presentation). Ranson criteria and BISAP score for severity. Management: aggressive IV fluid resuscitation (LR preferred over NS), NPO initially, IV analgesics (morphine OK), antiemetics. Early enteral nutrition within 24-48h (NG or NJ feeds). ERCP within 24h if gallstone pancreatitis with cholangitis or obstruction. CT with contrast at 48-72h if not improving to assess for necrosis/complications.

cases.hpi: {{patient_name}} is a child who presents with generalized weakness, oliguria, cola-colored (dark brown) urine, periorbital and ankle edema (2+ pitting), and hypertension 1-4 weeks after a streptococcal pharyngitis or skin infection (impetigo). This is acute poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis — an immune complex-mediated (type III hypersensitivity) disease. Antigen-antibody complexes deposit in the glomerular basement membrane → complement activation → glomerular inflammation. Labs: UA shows hematuria (dysmorphic RBCs, RBC casts — pathognomonic), proteinuria (<3.5g/day — nephritic, not nephrotic range). Low C3 complement (returns to normal in 6-8 weeks). Elevated ASO titer (pharyngitis) or anti-DNase B (skin infection). BMP shows elevated BUN/Cr (acute kidney injury). Diagnosis is clinical. Renal biopsy only if rapidly progressive GN or atypical course. Treatment: supportive — salt/fluid restriction, diuretics (furosemide) for hypertension and edema, antihypertensives if needed. Prognosis excellent in children (>95% complete recovery). Antibiotics if active strep infection. No immunosuppression needed.

cases.hpi: {{patient_name}} presents with acute onset severe monoarticular knee pain, erythema, warmth, and swelling. Pain began suddenly overnight — classic podagra (great toe) or knee involvement. History reveals dietary triggers (red meat, seafood, alcohol) or diuretic use. Gout is caused by monosodium urate crystal deposition in joints from chronic hyperuricemia. Definitive diagnosis: joint aspiration with synovial fluid analysis under polarized light microscopy — needle-shaped, negatively birefringent crystals. Do NOT give NSAIDs in renal impairment. First-line acute treatment: NSAIDs (indomethacin or naproxen), colchicine (within 36h of onset), or corticosteroids (oral prednisone or intra-articular injection). Colchicine: avoid in renal/hepatic impairment, CYP3A4 interactions. Long-term urate-lowering: allopurinol or febuxostat (start after acute flare resolves, with colchicine prophylaxis for 3-6 months). Target uric acid <6.0 mg/dL (or <5.0 for tophaceous gout).

cases.hpi: {{patient_name}} presents with acute monoarticular knee pain, fever, and chills. The knee is warm, swollen, erythematous, and exquisitely tender with limited range of motion. Disseminated gonococcal infection (DGI) is the most common cause of septic arthritis in sexually active young adults. Classic triad: tenosynovitis, dermatitis (pustular or vesiculopustular lesions), and migratory polyarthralgia progressing to monoarticular septic arthritis. Most commonly affects knee. Diagnosis: arthrocentesis with synovial fluid analysis (WBC >50,000, Gram stain may show Gram-negative diplococci, culture positive in only 50%). Also culture cervix, urethra, rectum, pharynx for N. gonorrhoeae. NAAT on synovial fluid. Treatment: ceftriaxone 1g IV daily initially, then switch to oral cefixime or fluoroquinolone based on sensitivities. If chlamydia co-infection possible (common), add doxycycline or azithromycin. Joint drainage (serial aspiration or arthroscopy). Partner treatment essential.

Giardia lamblia is a flagellated protozoan transmitted via fecal-oral route through contaminated water (common in hikers/campers — 'beaver fever'). Cysts are chlorine-resistant. cases.hpi: {{patient_name}} is found unresponsive with pinpoint pupils, respiratory depression (RR <12), and decreased bowel sounds — the classic opioid toxidrome. There may be needle track marks. Immediate management: airway protection, bag-valve-mask ventilation, naloxone 0.4-2mg IV/IM/IN (repeat q2-3min, up to 10mg if no response). Naloxone is a pure opioid antagonist — rapidly reverses respiratory depression but can precipitate acute withdrawal (agitation, vomiting, diarrhea, piloerection). Short half-life (30-90 min) compared to many opioids → patient may become re-sedated → need for observation or naloxone infusion. Check glucose (coma cocktail). ECG (QT prolongation with methadone). Acetaminophen and salicylate levels if polysubstance ingestion suspected. After stabilization: screen for other substances, assess for aspiration pneumonitis, evaluate for rhabdomyolysis (prolonged down time). Offer substance use disorder resources and naloxone prescription for harm reduction. Psychiatry/addiction medicine consult.

There may be needle track marks. Immediate management: airway protection, bag-valve-mask ventilation, naloxone 0.4-2mg IV/IM/IN (repeat q2-3min, up to 10mg if no response). Naloxone is a pure opioid antagonist — rapidly reverses respiratory depression but can precipitate acute withdrawal (agitation, vomiting, diarrhea, piloerection). Short half-life (30-90 min) compared to many opioids → patient may become re-sedated → need for observation or naloxone infusion. Check glucose (coma cocktail). ECG (QT prolongation with methadone). Acetaminophen and salicylate levels if polysubstance ingestion suspected. After stabilization: screen for other substances, assess for aspiration pneumonitis, evaluate for rhabdomyolysis (prolonged down time). cases.hpi: {{patient_name}} presents with rapidly progressive symmetric ascending weakness beginning in the lower extremities, areflexia, and possible paresthesias. History often reveals antecedent infection (Campylobacter jejuni most common, also viral URI, EBV, CMV) or vaccination within 1-4 weeks. GBS is an acute inflammatory demyelinating polyradiculoneuropathy (AIDP) caused by molecular mimicry — antibodies against infectious agents cross-react with peripheral nerve antigens. Classic: ascending symmetric weakness + areflexia + albuminocytologic dissociation in CSF (elevated protein with normal WBC count). EMG/NCS shows demyelinating pattern. Critical complication: respiratory failure from diaphragm involvement — monitor FVC and NIF (negative inspiratory force). FVC <20 mL/kg or NIF <-30 cm H2O = elective intubation. Autonomic instability common (labile BP, arrhythmias). Treatment: IVIG (0.4g/kg/day x 5 days) or plasmapheresis — both equally effective. Do NOT give steroids (ineffective in GBS, unlike CIDP). ICU admission for monitoring. Prognosis: 85% recover, 3-5% mortality.

cases.hpi: {{patient_name}} presents with severe unilateral orbital/supraorbital/temporal headache lasting 15-180 minutes, occurring in clusters (multiple times per day for weeks-months then remission). Associated ipsilateral autonomic features: lacrimation, conjunctival injection, nasal congestion, rhinorrhea, eyelid edema, miosis/ptosis (Horner's). Patient is restless/agitated during attacks (unlike migraine where patient lies still). Triggers: alcohol during cluster period. More common in men. First-line acute treatment: high-flow 100% oxygen 12-15 L/min via non-rebreather (aborts attack within 15 min) AND/OR subcutaneous sumatriptan 6mg. cases.hpi: {{patient_name}} presents with transient focal neurological deficit (unilateral weakness, aphasia, visual field defect) resolving completely within 24 hours (typically <1 hour). Exam reveals carotid bruit on the right. TIA is a neurological emergency — 10-15% risk of stroke within 90 days, highest in first 48 hours. ABCD2 score predicts stroke risk. Workup: non-contrast head CT (rule out hemorrhage), carotid duplex ultrasound (identify stenosis — this patient has right carotid bruit), ECG (atrial fibrillation is common cause), echocardiogram (cardioembolic source), MRI brain (DWI for ischemia). Aggressive risk factor management: statin, BP control, diabetes control, smoking cessation. Admit for expedited workup.

cases.hpi: {{patient_name}} is a term newborn presenting with jaundice appearing after day 3-5 of life, clinically well-appearing, feeding well, gaining weight appropriately. Breastfeeding jaundice is the most common cause of prolonged neonatal unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia. Pathophysiology: inadequate breastfeeding intake → decreased stooling → increased enterohepatic circulation of bilirubin. Must distinguish from pathologic causes: hemolysis (ABO/Rh incompatibility, G6PD deficiency), sepsis, biliary atresia (conjugated), hypothyroidism. Key labs: total and direct bilirubin (unconjugated > conjugated by definition), CBC with reticulocyte count (anemia? hemolysis?), direct Coombs (immune hemolysis), G6PD screen. Plot on Bhutani nomogram for phototherapy threshold. Management: optimize breastfeeding (increase frequency, lactation consultation). Phototherapy if bilirubin exceeds threshold for gestational age and risk factors. Exchange transfusion if signs of bilirubin encephalopathy or failed phototherapy.

cases.hpi: {{patient_name}} presents with acute abdominal/back pain, fatigue, jaundice, and dark urine (hemoglobinuria) following exposure to an oxidative stressor (fava beans, infection, certain drugs: sulfa, primaquine, dapsone, nitrofurantoin, rasburicase). Labs show acute hemolytic anemia (low Hb, elevated LDH, low haptoglobin, elevated reticulocyte count, indirect hyperbilirubinemia). Peripheral smear shows bite cells, blister cells, and Heinz bodies. G6PD deficiency is the most common enzymopathy worldwide — X-linked recessive. G6PD protects RBCs from oxidative stress. Trigger → oxidative damage → intravascular + extravascular hemolysis. Diagnosis: G6PD enzyme assay (do NOT check during acute hemolysis — reticulocytes have higher G6PD). Treatment: supportive — remove trigger, IV fluids, transfuse if severe anemia. Avoid oxidative drugs lifelong. Screen family members (X-linked).

cases.hpi: {{patient_name}} is a child (commonly 6 months - 3 years) presenting with acute severe colicky abdominal pain occurring in episodes, with drawing up of knees, and currant jelly stools (blood and mucus). Between episodes the child may appear normal. A sausage-shaped mass may be palpable in the RLQ (intussusception of terminal ileum into cecum — most common type). Intussusception is the most common cause of intestinal obstruction in children <2 years. Peak incidence 6-12 months. Often preceded by viral illness (rotavirus, adenovirus). Diagnostic test of choice: abdominal ultrasound (target sign/doughnut sign on transverse view). Treatment: therapeutic air or contrast enema (reduces the intussusception in 80-90%). Do NOT attempt enema if perforation (free air on X-ray). Surgical reduction if enema fails or perforation present. NPO and NG tube for decompression. IV fluids for resuscitation.

cases.hpi: {{patient_name}} is a child (6 months - 3 years) presenting with acute onset barky cough, inspiratory stridor, hoarseness, and respiratory distress, worse at night. Often preceded by viral URI (parainfluenza virus type 1 most common). Croup is inflammation of the larynx and subglottic airway. Westley croup score assesses severity based on stridor, retractions, air entry, cyanosis, and level of consciousness. Classic CXR finding: steeple sign (subglottic narrowing on AP view). Treatment: mild (no stridor at rest) = supportive care, cool mist. Moderate to severe = dexamethasone 0.6 mg/kg PO/IM once ± nebulized racemic epinephrine. Dexamethasone reduces airway edema. Racemic epinephrine is for temporary relief only — observe 2-4 hours after administration for rebound. Hospitalize if requiring racemic epinephrine, stridor at rest, hypoxia, or dehydration. Avoid unnecessary agitation — keep child calm.

cases.hpi: {{patient_name}} presents with acute severe unilateral flank pain radiating to the groin, associated with nausea, vomiting, and hematuria. Pain is colicky — comes in waves as the stone passes. Non-contrast CT abdomen/pelvis is the gold standard for diagnosis. Ultrasound can be used in pregnancy/children. UA shows microscopic or gross hematuria. Most stones are calcium oxalate. Treatment depends on size and location: <5-10mm stones at UVJ or distal ureter → medical expulsive therapy (tamsulosin) + analgesia + IV fluids. Larger stones or proximal location → urology consult for lithotripsy or ureteroscopy. Strain urine and send stone for analysis. Metabolic workup if recurrent. Prevention: increase fluid intake (>2L/day), dietary modifications based on stone type.

cases.hpi: {{patient_name}} presents with bilateral, pressing/tightening (non-pulsating), mild to moderate intensity headache without nausea, vomiting, photophobia, or phonophobia. No aura. Not aggravated by routine physical activity. Duration 30 min to 7 days. Tension headache is the most common primary headache disorder — bilateral, band-like pressure. Distinguish from migraine (unilateral, pulsating, moderate-severe, nausea/photophobia, aggravated by activity) and cluster (unilateral with autonomic features). No imaging needed if history/neuro exam normal. Treatment: acute — NSAIDs (ibuprofen, naproxen) or acetaminophen. Avoid opioid and butalbital-containing analgesics (rebound headache risk). Prophylaxis if frequent: amitriptyline, nortriptyline (TCAs first-line). Non-pharmacologic: stress management, trigger avoidance, relaxation techniques, biofeedback.

cases.hpi: {{patient_name}} presents with witnessed generalized tonic-clonic seizure: sudden loss of consciousness, tonic phase (stiffening), clonic phase (rhythmic jerking), post-ictal confusion/drowsiness. Tongue laceration and urinary incontinence are common. First unprovoked seizure requires thorough workup: CT/MRI brain (structural lesion), EEG (epileptiform discharges, classify seizure type), labs (CBC, BMP, glucose, tox screen, LP if infection suspected). Alcohol withdrawal, electrolyte abnormalities (hypoNa, hypoMg, hypoCa), hypoglycemia, and CNS infection are common triggers. Do NOT start anti-epileptic drugs after single unprovoked seizure unless high risk (abnormal EEG, structural lesion, family history). Driving restrictions per state law. If recurrent seizures or high risk → start AED (levetiracetam, lamotrigine, valproic acid). Status epilepticus: >5 min of continuous seizure or recurrent without return to baseline = medical emergency (IV lorazepam/diazepam).

cases.hpi: {{patient_name}} presents with vague abdominal/pelvic discomfort, early satiety, bloating, increased abdominal girth, urinary frequency, and unintentional weight loss — classic insidious presentation of ovarian cancer. Exam may reveal pelvic mass, ascites, omental cake. Ovarian cancer is the leading cause of gynecologic cancer death because it presents late. Workup: transvaginal ultrasound (first-line imaging — adnexal mass, complex cystic-solid, ascites), CA-125 tumor marker (elevated in 80% of advanced ovarian cancer, but not diagnostic — also elevated in endometriosis, PID, fibroids), CT abdomen/pelvis for staging. Definitive diagnosis: surgical exploration with staging laparotomy (TAH-BSO, omentectomy, lymph node sampling). Refer to gynecologic oncology. BRCA testing if family history (germline BRCA1/2 in ~15%).

cases.hpi: {{patient_name}} is a child presenting with abdominal pain, constipation, irritability, lethargy, ataxia, and cognitive changes. History reveals exposure to lead-based paint in older home (built <1978). Lead intoxication causes microcytic anemia with basophilic stippling on peripheral smear. Elevated free erythrocyte protoporphyrin (FEP). Definitive diagnosis: blood lead level (BLL) >5 mcg/dL is elevated. >45 mcg/dL requires chelation. >70 mcg/dL is a medical emergency. Chronic lead exposure affects: nervous system (encephalopathy, developmental delay), kidneys (Fanconi syndrome), bone marrow (anemia), GI (colic). Treatment: remove source (lead abatement). Chelation therapy: succimer (DMSA) PO for BLL >45, or IV edetate calcium disodium (EDTA) + dimercaprol (BAL) for lead encephalopathy (BLL >70). Iron supplementation for anemia. Report to public health.

cases.chief_complaint: Anxiety with palpitations, tremor, and sweating
cases.case_summary:
Differential: Anxiety, Atrial fibrillation, Early menopause, Mitral valve prolapse, Panic attack, Withdrawal syndrome, Stimulant intoxication.

The patient in this case has Graves' hyperthyroidism with a very clear history and classic physical exam findings (tremor, sweating, pretibial myxedema, exophthalmos). The best way to treat this patient is to start both symptomatic treatment with a beta-blocker (propranolol) and an antithyroid medication such as methimazole or PTU. Both are acceptable, but methimazole is almost always the first-line choice with the exception of the first trimester of pregnancy, during which PTU is preferred, due to methimazole's teratogenicity. This is why it's important to order a urine pregnancy test on this patient prior to treatment. Surgery and radioiodine ablation are alternative options to treat Graves' hyperthyroidism, but it's important to know that patients with significant symptoms of hyperthyroidism (such as this patient) need to be treated with antithyroid medications and achieve a euthyroid state before either of these other treatment options are pursued.

cases.hpi: {{patient_name}} presents with chronic cough >3 weeks, hemoptysis, night sweats, weight loss, fever, and fatigue. Risk factors: immigration from endemic area, HIV, homelessness, incarceration, healthcare exposure. TB is caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis — acid-fast bacillus. CXR: apical infiltrates, cavitary lesions (reactivation TB), hilar lymphadenopathy, Ghon complex (primary). Diagnosis: sputum AFB smear (rapid, less sensitive), NAAT (PCR), mycobacterial culture (gold standard, results in weeks). IGRA (QuantiFERON) or PPD for latent TB screening — positive in active and latent. Airborne isolation (negative pressure room, N95). Treatment: RIPE therapy — Rifampin, Isoniazid, Pyrazinamide, Ethambutol for 2 months then INH + rifampin for 4 months. Directly observed therapy (DOT) preferred. Monitor LFTs (hepatotoxicity), vision (ethambutol → optic neuritis). Vitamin B6 (pyridoxine) with INH to prevent neuropathy. Report to public health.

cases.hpi: {{patient_name}} presents with urinary frequency, urgency, nocturia, weak stream, hesitancy, straining, and sensation of incomplete bladder emptying — classic LUTS (lower urinary tract symptoms) in an older man. DRE reveals enlarged, smooth, non-tender prostate. BPH is caused by benign proliferation of prostatic stromal and epithelial tissue, causing urethral compression. AUA symptom score quantifies severity. Labs: UA (rule out UTI), BMP (Cr — assess for obstructive nephropathy), PSA (age-appropriate screening). If mild: watchful waiting, lifestyle modifications. If moderate-severe: medical therapy — alpha-blockers (tamsulosin, alfuzosin — relax smooth muscle, rapid onset) ± 5-alpha reductase inhibitors (finasteride, dutasteride — shrink prostate, slow onset, reduce risk of urinary retention and surgery). Combination therapy for significant symptoms. Surgery (TURP) if refractory. Avoid anticholinergics and decongestants.

cases.hpi: {{patient_name}} presents with progressive proximal muscle weakness, myalgias, and fatigue. History reveals concurrent use of simvastatin and gemfibrozil — a CONTRAINDICATED combination. Gemfibrozil inhibits CYP2C8 and OATP1B1, dramatically increasing simvastatin levels → myotoxicity. Labs show markedly elevated CK (often >10x ULN). UA shows myoglobinuria (risk of AKI). Differentiate from other causes: hypothyroidism, polymyositis, alcohol myopathy, steroid myopathy. Management: IMMEDIATELY discontinue simvastatin and gemfibrozil. Aggressive IV fluids to prevent pigment nephropathy from rhabdomyolysis. Monitor renal function and electrolytes (hyperkalemia risk from muscle breakdown). Alternative lipid management after recovery: atorvastatin or rosuvastatin (metabolized differently, less interaction risk), ezetimibe, PCSK9 inhibitor. Fenofibrate (not gemfibrozil) can be used with statins with caution.

cases.hpi: {{patient_name}} presents with acute onset unilateral leg pain, erythema, warmth, swelling, and fever. The affected area shows poorly demarcated erythema, warmth, and edema. Cellulitis is an infection of the deep dermis and subcutaneous tissue — most commonly caused by beta-hemolytic Streptococci (Group A Strep) and S. aureus. Differentiate from erysipelas (more superficial, well-demarcated, raised borders). Risk factors: skin breaks, tinea pedis, lymphedema, venous stasis, diabetes, immunocompromise. Portal of entry must be identified. Mark the borders of erythema to monitor progression. Treatment: oral antibiotics for mild-moderate (cephalexin, dicloxacillin, clindamycin if penicillin-allergic). IV antibiotics for severe/systemic symptoms (cefazolin, nafcillin, vancomycin if MRSA risk). Elevate affected limb. Treat underlying predisposing conditions.

cases.hpi: {{patient_name}} presents with chronic diarrhea, steatorrhea, bloating, abdominal pain, weight loss, fatigue, and iron deficiency anemia. Celiac disease is an autoimmune enteropathy triggered by gluten in genetically susceptible individuals (HLA-DQ2/DQ8). Gliadin peptides are deamidated by tissue transglutaminase (tTG) → immune response → small intestinal villous atrophy. Classic extra-intestinal manifestations: dermatitis herpetiformis (pruritic vesicles on extensor surfaces), iron deficiency anemia, osteoporosis, peripheral neuropathy. Diagnosis: IgA anti-tTG antibody (first-line serology) + total IgA level (rule out IgA deficiency, which causes false-negative tTG). If IgA deficient, use IgG anti-tTG or anti-DGP. Confirm with duodenal biopsy showing villous atrophy, crypt hyperplasia, intraepithelial lymphocytosis (gold standard). DO NOT start gluten-free diet before biopsy. Treatment: lifelong strict gluten-free diet. Monitor nutritional deficiencies (iron, B12, folate, vitamin D, calcium).

cases.hpi: {{patient_name}} presents with palpitations, irregularly irregular pulse, dizziness, fatigue, and chest discomfort. ECG shows no P waves, irregularly irregular R-R intervals with narrow QRS. May have rapid ventricular response (RVR). AFib is the most common sustained cardiac arrhythmia. Causes: HTN, CAD, valvular disease, CHF, hyperthyroidism, alcohol, PE, post-op, lone AFib. Classification: paroxysmal (<7d), persistent (>7d), long-standing persistent (>1yr), permanent. Management priorities: (1) Rate control: beta-blocker (metoprolol) or CCB (diltiazem/verapamil), target HR <110. (3) Rhythm control if symptomatic despite rate control: cardioversion (electrical or pharmacological — flecainide, amiodarone). If AFib <48h → safe to cardiovert. If >48h or unknown → TEE to rule out LAA thrombus first, or anticoagulate x3 weeks before cardioversion. Anticoagulate x4 weeks post-cardioversion.

cases.hpi: {{patient_name}} is a neonate/infant presenting with bilious (green) vomiting — a surgical emergency until proven otherwise. Bilious vomiting in a newborn = malrotation with volvulus. Malrotation occurs when the midgut fails to complete its normal 270° counterclockwise rotation during fetal development, resulting in a narrow mesenteric base. This predisposes to volvulus — twisting of the midgut around the superior mesenteric artery → intestinal ischemia and necrosis. Diagnosis: upper GI series (gold standard) showing DJJ (duodenojejunal junction) to the RIGHT of midline and spiral/corkscrew duodenum. Abdominal X-ray may show double bubble sign or gasless abdomen. Treatment: EMERGENCY surgical exploration (Ladd procedure). NPO, NG tube decompression, IV fluids. Time-critical — delay leads to bowel necrosis and short gut syndrome.

cases.title: Diarrhea

rationale.Colonoscopy + biopsy: Skip lesions, cobblestoning, transmural inflammation, non-caseating granulomas.

cases.hpi: {{patient_name}} presents with chronic diarrhea (often non-bloody), RLQ abdominal pain, weight loss, fatigue, and fever. Crohn's disease is a transmural granulomatous inflammatory bowel disease that can affect any part of the GI tract from mouth to anus — most commonly terminal ileum. Skip lesions (areas of inflammation between normal mucosa), cobblestoning, creeping fat, strictures, and fistulas are characteristic. Extraintestinal manifestations: arthritis, uveitis, erythema nodosum, pyoderma gangrenosum, PSC. cases.hpi: {{patient_name}} is an elderly patient with cardiovascular risk factors who presents with acute LLQ abdominal pain and bloody diarrhea following a meal (postprandial pain). Ischemic colitis is the most common form of GI ischemia — caused by non-occlusive hypoperfusion of the watershed areas (splenic flexure = Griffith's point, rectosigmoid = Sudeck's point). Differentiate from acute mesenteric ischemia (small bowel — embolic, more severe, pain out of proportion). CT abdomen/pelvis with IV contrast shows segmental colonic wall thickening, thumbprinting (submucosal edema/hemorrhage). Colonoscopy confirms with segmental erythema, ulceration. Most cases are self-limited and resolve with supportive care: bowel rest (NPO), IV fluids, broad-spectrum antibiotics (cover gram-neg + anaerobes if severe). Surgery only if transmural infarction, perforation, peritonitis, or stricture.

cases.hpi: {{patient_name}} presents with oligomenorrhea/amenorrhea, hirsutism, acne, obesity, and infertility. PCOS is the most common endocrine disorder in reproductive-age women. Rotterdam criteria (need 2 of 3): (1) oligo/anovulation, (2) clinical or biochemical hyperandrogenism (hirsutism, acne, elevated free testosterone), (3) polycystic ovaries on ultrasound (≥12 follicles 2-9mm per ovary or ovarian volume >10mL). Other causes of hyperandrogenism must be ruled out: late-onset CAH (check 17-OH progesterone), androgen-secreting tumor (rapid virilization, very high testosterone), Cushing's, hyperprolactinemia. Labs: LH:FSH ratio >2:1 is classic but not diagnostic. Associated with insulin resistance → screen for diabetes (glucose, HbA1c, OGTT). Treatment: weight loss (first-line, improves all parameters), combined OCPs (regulate cycles, reduce hyperandrogenism), metformin (insulin sensitizer, improves ovulation), spironolactone (anti-androgen for hirsutism). Clomiphene or letrozole for ovulation induction if fertility desired.

cases.hpi: {{patient_name}} presents with hematuria, flank pain, hypertension, and palpable bilateral flank masses. Family history of ADPKD (autosomal dominant — 50% of children inherit). ADPKD is the most common inherited kidney disease — mutations in PKD1 (85%, chromosome 16) or PKD2 (15%, chromosome 4). Cysts develop in kidneys (and liver, pancreas) over decades, eventually causing renal failure by age 50-60. Diagnosis: renal ultrasound — multiple bilateral cysts in enlarged kidneys (usually by age 30 for PKD1). CT/MRI for more detail. Labs: elevated Cr (declining renal function), UA shows hematuria. Screen for cerebral aneurysms (berry aneurysms — 5-10% of ADPKD patients, higher if family history) with MRA/CTA brain. Management: BP control with ACEI/ARB (nephroprotective), treat UTIs aggressively, avoid contact sports (cyst rupture risk). Tolvaptan (vasopressin antagonist) slows cyst growth. Genetic counseling.

cases.hpi: {{patient_name}} presents with chronic bloody diarrhea, LLQ abdominal cramping, tenesmus, urgency, and weight loss. UC is an inflammatory bowel disease limited to the colon and rectum — inflammation is continuous from the rectum proximally (unlike Crohn's skip lesions), limited to mucosa/submucosa (unlike Crohn's transmural). Extraintestinal manifestations: PSC (most specific), arthritis (axial/peripheral), uveitis, erythema nodosum, pyoderma gangrenosum. Diagnosis: colonoscopy with biopsy — continuous inflammation from rectum, friable mucosa, loss of haustra (lead pipe colon on barium enema), crypt abscesses, crypt distortion. Labs: anemia, elevated CRP/ESR, fecal calprotectin, p-ANCA positive. Severity determines treatment: mild → 5-ASA (mesalamine) topical or PO. Moderate → 5-ASA + steroids (prednisone or budesonide MMX). Severe → IV steroids, if refractory → biologics (anti-TNF — infliximab) or JAK inhibitor (tofacitinib). Fulminant/toxic megacolon → cyclosporine or colectomy. Increased colon cancer risk → surveillance colonoscopy starting 8 years after diagnosis.

cases.hpi: {{patient_name}} is a pregnant woman >20 weeks gestation with elevated BP (>140/90 on two occasions at least 4 hours apart) and no proteinuria and no end-organ damage. This is gestational hypertension (PIH) — distinguished from pre-eclampsia by absence of proteinuria and end-organ dysfunction. Risk factors: nulliparity, advanced maternal age, obesity, family history, multiple gestation. Must monitor closely for progression to pre-eclampsia (up to 25% progress). Management: if BP >160/110 → antihypertensive treatment (labetalol, nifedipine ER, methyldopa). If BP 140-159/90-109 → conservative monitoring, no medication needed but close surveillance. ACEI/ARBs CONTRAINDICATED in pregnancy. Serial monitoring: BP checks, UA for protein, fetal growth US, NST/BPP starting at 32 weeks. Delivery at 37 weeks (no later than term). If develops pre-eclampsia features → manage as pre-eclampsia. Low-dose aspirin 81mg for pre-eclampsia prevention in high-risk women (started at 12-28 weeks).

cases.hpi: {{patient_name}} presents with malar (butterfly) rash across cheeks (sparing nasolabial folds), photosensitivity, polyarthritis, fatigue, and fever. SLE is a multisystem autoimmune disease with autoantibodies against nuclear antigens. Diagnosis per ACR/EULAR criteria: ANA positivity is required (sensitive but not specific). Anti-dsDNA and anti-Smith are specific for SLE. Other features: oral ulcers, serositis (pleuritis/pericarditis), nephritis (proteinuria, RBC casts), neurologic (seizures/psychosis), hematologic (anemia, leukopenia, lymphopenia, thrombocytopenia). Monitor: CBC, BMP, UA (proteinuria), complement C3/C4 (low = active disease), anti-dsDNA titers (correlates with disease activity). Treatment: mild (skin/joints) → hydroxychloroquine (ALL SLE patients) + NSAIDs. Moderate: add steroids (prednisone). Severe (nephritis, CNS) → high-dose steroids + immunosuppression (mycophenolate mofetil or cyclophosphamide). Sun protection.

cases.hpi: {{patient_name}} presents with vaginal bleeding, cramping lower abdominal pain, and passage of tissue in early pregnancy (<20 weeks). Types: threatened (bleeding, closed os, viable fetus), inevitable (bleeding, open os), incomplete (partial passage of tissue, open os), complete (all tissue passed, os closed), missed (fetal demise without expulsion). Diagnosis: HCG positive, transvaginal ultrasound to assess fetal cardiac activity, gestational sac, and retained products. Serial HCG levels: normally doubles every 48h in early pregnancy — falling or plateauing suggests nonviable pregnancy. If Rh-negative → Rhogam (anti-D immune globulin) to prevent alloimmunization. Treatment: threatened → expectant management, pelvic rest. Inevitable/incomplete: expectant (allow to pass), medical (misoprostol), or surgical (D&C). Complete → confirm with US, no further treatment needed. Emotional support and counseling.

Menopause = 12 months of amenorrhea. Genitourinary syndrome of menopause (atrophic vaginitis): thinning and drying of vaginal mucosa from estrogen loss → dyspareunia, pruritus, increased UTIs. cases.hpi: {{patient_name}} presents with acute low back pain radiating down the leg (sciatica) following lifting/twisting injury. Pain follows dermatomal distribution — most commonly L4-L5 or L5-S1. Exam: positive straight leg raise test (pain <70° elevation). Neurologic exam to identify affected root: L4 (patellar reflex, medial leg), L5 (foot drop, great toe dorsiflexion, dorsal foot), S1 (Achilles reflex, plantar flexion, lateral foot). Cauda equina RED FLAGS: bilateral sciatica, saddle anesthesia, urinary retention/incontinence, fecal incontinence — surgical emergency. Conservative management for uncomplicated herniation: NSAIDs, physical therapy, continue activity as tolerated (bed rest NOT recommended). Most resolve in 6 weeks. MRI if not improving or neurologic deficit (not urgent CT/bone scan — but MRI is gold standard). Epidural steroid injection for radicular pain. Surgery (microdiscectomy) if severe deficit, cauda equina, or failed 6+ weeks conservative.

cases.hpi: {{patient_name}} presents with severe low back pain, bilateral leg weakness and numbness, saddle anesthesia (perineal numbness), urinary retention/incontinence, fecal incontinence, and decreased rectal tone. These are the RED FLAG symptoms of cauda equina syndrome — compression of the cauda equina nerve roots below the conus medullaris. This is a SURGICAL EMERGENCY. Delay in decompression leads to permanent paralysis, incontinence, and sexual dysfunction. Most common cause: massive central disc herniation. Other causes: trauma, tumor, abscess, hematoma. Diagnosis: EMERGENCY MRI of lumbar spine (do NOT wait). Post-void residual (PVR) >200mL supports diagnosis. Treatment: EMERGENCY neurosurgical decompression (laminectomy + discectomy) within 24-48 hours of symptom onset.

cases.hpi: {{patient_name}} presents with acute onset high fever, severe sore throat, drooling, muffled 'hot potato' voice, stridor, and tripod positioning (leaning forward, chin thrust out). Epiglottitis is a life-threatening airway emergency. Historically caused by H. influenzae type B (now rare due to Hib vaccine) — now more commonly Group A Strep, S. pneumoniae, Staph. Do NOT examine the throat or agitate the child — can trigger complete airway obstruction! Let the child remain in position of comfort. Immediate management: keep child calm, avoid invasive exam, arrange for controlled airway management in OR by anesthesia/ENT (awake fiberoptic intubation). Croup (laryngotracheitis) is viral, slower onset, barky cough — epiglottitis is rapid, toxic-appearing, no cough. Lateral neck X-ray shows 'thumbprint sign' (swollen epiglottis) but do NOT send child to radiology unattended. Treatment: IV antibiotics (ceftriaxone + vancomycin), steroids (dexamethasone).

cases.hpi: {{patient_name}} presents with episodes of confusion, diaphoresis, tremors, palpitations, and generalized weakness — relieved by eating (Whipple's triad: hypoglycemic symptoms + low glucose <50 mg/dL + relief with glucose administration). Insulinoma is a neuroendocrine tumor of pancreatic beta cells causing inappropriate insulin secretion → fasting hypoglycemia. Diagnosis: supervised 72-hour fast — will develop hypoglycemia with inappropriately elevated insulin + C-peptide levels (endogenous insulin). Insulin:glucose ratio elevated. Sulfonylurea screen negative (rules out factitious hypoglycemia). Localization: CT/MRI abdomen, endoscopic ultrasound, or selective arterial calcium stimulation. Treatment: surgical resection (enucleation). If unresectable or metastatic: diazoxide (suppresses insulin secretion), octreotide, everolimus. Frequent small meals, avoid prolonged fasting.

cases.hpi: {{patient_name}} presents with localized lower back pain, fever, chills, malaise, and point tenderness over the affected vertebrae. Vertebral osteomyelitis is a bacterial infection of the vertebral body — most commonly S. aureus. Risk factors: IV drug use, recent bacteremia, indwelling catheters, DM, immunocompromised. Diagnosis: MRI spine with contrast (gold standard — high sensitivity). Plain X-ray may be normal early (need 30-50% bone loss to see). Blood cultures x2 (positive in 50%). If blood cultures negative → CT-guided or open biopsy for culture. ESR and CRP elevated. Treatment: IV antibiotics (empiric: vancomycin + ceftriaxone or cefepime — cover MRSA and gram-negatives) x 6 weeks minimum, tailored to culture results. Surgical debridement if abscess, neurologic deficit, spinal instability, or failure of medical therapy.

cases.hpi: {{patient_name}} presents with acute onset severe unilateral pelvic/abdominal pain following activity (intercourse, exercise). May have vaginal bleeding. Exam reveals peritoneal signs, adnexal tenderness, possible palpable mass. Ruptured ovarian cyst → bleeding into peritoneal cavity → hemoperitoneum → hypovolemia and acute abdomen. Most common: ruptured corpus luteum cyst. Differential: ectopic pregnancy (MUST rule out — HCG), PID, appendicitis, ovarian torsion. Diagnosis: HCG negative (rules out ectopic). Transvaginal ultrasound shows free fluid in pelvis/abdomen, ruptured cyst, possible adnexal mass. CBC for anemia from blood loss. Type and screen. Management: stable → observation, analgesia, serial hematocrit. Unstable/hypotensive → IV fluids, blood transfusion if needed, surgical consult (laparoscopy vs laparotomy for hemostasis). If on anticoagulation → reverse.

cases.title: Fatigue
cases.hpi: {{patient_name}} presents with fever (single temp >38.3°C or sustained >38.0°C for 1h) and absolute neutrophil count <500 cells/µL. This is a MEDICAL EMERGENCY — mortality high without immediate antibiotics. Most commonly seen post-chemotherapy. Often no localizing signs of infection because there are no neutrophils to create pus/inflammation. Blood cultures x2, UA + culture, CXR. Calculate MASCC score for risk stratification (low-risk may be outpatient). Treatment: empiric IV antibiotics within 1 HOUR — monotherapy with anti-pseudomonal beta-lactam (cefepime, meropenem, pip-tazo). Add vancomycin if: hemodynamic instability, suspected catheter infection, skin/soft tissue infection, known MRSA colonization, severe mucositis. If persists >4-7 days → add antifungal coverage. G-CSF may be considered. Admit. Reverse isolation (neutropenic precautions).
