cases.hpi: {{patient_name}} presents with paranoia, auditory hallucinations (hearing voices), disorganized speech/behavior, negative symptoms (flat affect, social withdrawal, avolition), and functional decline >6 months. Schizophrenia is a chronic psychiatric disorder — symptoms for ≥6 months with ≥1 month of active symptoms. Must rule out substance-induced psychosis, medical causes (CNS tumor, infection, autoimmune encephalitis, thyroid), and other psychiatric disorders (bipolar with psychosis, schizoaffective). Diagnosis is clinical — no diagnostic test. Collateral history crucial. Treatment: antipsychotics (second-generation: risperidone, olanzapine, quetiapine, aripiprazole — fewer EPS than first-gen like haloperidol). Clozapine for treatment-resistant. Monitor for metabolic syndrome (weight, glucose, lipids). Long-acting injectables for non-adherence. Psychosocial interventions: CBT, family therapy, supported employment. Safety assessment for self-harm/aggression.

cases.hpi: {{patient_name}} presents unresponsive with respiratory depression, CNS depression, and hypotonia. Pupils may be normal or slightly constricted (unlike opioid pinpoint). History of diazepam use confirmed. Benzo overdose alone rarely causes death unless mixed with other sedatives (alcohol, opioids). Flumazenil is a competitive benzodiazepine antagonist — but use with EXTREME CAUTION. Flumazenil can precipitate acute withdrawal seizures, especially in chronic benzo users or mixed overdose with TCAs. Generally NOT recommended for routine use. Treatment: supportive care — airway protection (intubate if needed), respiratory support, IV fluids, observation. Decontamination with activated charcoal if recent ingestion (<1h) and airway protected. Full recovery expected with supportive care alone for isolated benzo overdose. Toxicology screen to rule out co-ingestants. Psychiatry consult for intentional overdose.

cases.hpi: {{patient_name}} presents with rash, lymphadenopathy, and possible genital lesion history. Secondary syphilis: diffuse maculopapular rash (INCLUDING palms and soles — key differentiating feature), condyloma lata (wart-like lesions in moist areas), lymphadenopathy, flu-like symptoms. Primary syphilis: painless indurated chancre at inoculation site (resolves spontaneously). Caused by Treponema pallidum (spirochete). Diagnosis: screening with RPR or VDRL (non-treponemal — titer correlates with disease activity). Confirm with treponemal-specific test (FTA-ABS, TP-PA). Darkfield microscopy of chancre fluid can directly visualize spirochetes. HIV testing (high co-infection). Treatment: benzathine penicillin G 2.4M units IM once (primary/secondary/early latent). Doxycycline if penicillin-allergic. Jarisch-Herxheimer reaction may occur (fever, myalgias, headache within 24h). Report to public health. Partner notification. Follow RPR titers to confirm cure (4-fold decline).

cases.hpi: {{patient_name}} presents with acute onset dyspnea, tachypnea, hypoxemia, petechial rash (chest, axillae, conjunctivae), and CNS changes (confusion, AMS) 24-72 hours after a long bone fracture (femur, tibia) or pelvic fracture. Fat embolism syndrome is caused by fat globules from bone marrow entering venous circulation → lodged in pulmonary and cerebral capillaries → mechanical obstruction + inflammatory cascade. Triad: respiratory distress + petechial rash + CNS dysfunction. Diagnosis is clinical (no gold standard test). CXR may show diffuse bilateral infiltrates (ARDS pattern). ABG: hypoxemia, A-a gradient elevated. UA may show fat globules in urine. Treatment: SUPPORTIVE — oxygen, respiratory support (may require mechanical ventilation). Early surgical fixation of long bone fractures reduces risk. Maintain adequate oxygenation and hemodynamics.

rationale.STI testing + toxicology screen: CT/GC, HIV, syphilis, Hep B/C. Tox for DFSA.

cases.hpi: {{patient_name}} presents found unconscious with signs of physical struggle (bruises, abrasions, torn clothing). Management requires a multidisciplinary, trauma-informed approach. Priorities: medical stabilization first (ABCs), then forensic examination. Obtain consent before any exam. Sexual Assault Nurse Examiner (SANE) if available. Forensic evidence collection (rape kit): clothing, swabs, fingernail scrapings, hair samples — ideally within 72h. Document injuries with photographs. Labs: STI testing (chlamydia, gonorrhea, HIV, syphilis, hepatitis), pregnancy test, toxicology screen (drug-facilitated assault —GHB, benzodiazepines, ketamine). Empiric treatment: ceftriaxone + doxycycline + metronidazole for STI prophylaxis. Emergency contraception (levonorgestrel 1.5mg PO once). HIV PEP if within 72h. Report to law enforcement (with consent). Arrange safe discharge and follow-up. Psychiatry/crisis counseling referral.

cases.title: Drowning

rationale.ABCs / Oxygen / Airway: Intubate if hypoxic, unable to protect airway.

cases.hpi: {{patient_name}} is a child who was submerged in water, presenting with respiratory distress, hypoxia, altered mental status after water rescue. Drowning = respiratory impairment from submersion in liquid. Outcome: death, survival with morbidity, or survival without morbidity. NOT 'near-drowning' in current terminology. Fresh water vs salt water distinction clinically irrelevant — both cause pulmonary surfactant washout → ARDS. Key: hypoxic brain injury determines prognosis. Management: ABCs, oxygen, BVM or intubation if needed. C-spine precautions if diving mechanism. CXR (pulmonary edema vs aspiration pneumonia). Rewarming if hypothermic. All drowning victims need observation — even asymptomatic can deteriorate (secondary drowning from pulmonary edema). Admit for observation. Prevention counseling.

cases.title: Agitation
cases.hpi: {{patient_name}} presents with acute agitation, aggression, psychomotor activation, and possible threatening behavior. Priority: ensure safety of patient and staff. Determine etiology: psychiatric (schizophrenia, bipolar mania, psychosis) vs substance-induced (stimulants, PCP, alcohol withdrawal) vs medical (hypoglycemia, hypoxia, head injury, sepsis, encephalopathy). Rapid assessment: vital signs, fingerstick glucose, pulse oximetry, brief neuro exam. Verbal de-escalation first-line. If pharmacologic needed: PO preferred over IM if patient willing — lorazepam (benzo) or olanzapine (antipsychotic). If IM required: midazolam + haloperidol or olanzapine IM. Avoid physical restraints unless absolutely necessary — can worsen agitation and cause rhabdomyolysis. If restraints used: 1:1 observation, frequent monitoring. Once stabilized → workup for underlying cause (tox screen, CT head, labs). Psychiatry consult.

cases.title: Muscle Pain

rationale.BMP / UA / Ca / Phos: AKI, hyperK, hyperP, hypoCa. UA: blood+, no RBCs.
rationale.Treat hyperkalemia: Calcium gluconate, insulin+glucose, bicarb if severe.

cases.hpi: {{patient_name}} presents with diffuse muscle pain, weakness, dark cola-colored urine (myoglobinuria), and fatigue following prolonged immobilization, crush injury, extreme exertion, or medication reaction. Labs: markedly elevated CK (often >5,000, can be >100,000), elevated Cr (AKI from myoglobin), hyperkalemia, hyperphosphatemia, hypocalcemia. UA positive for blood on dipstick but no RBCs on microscopy (myoglobinuria). Rhabdomyolysis = skeletal muscle breakdown → release of intracellular contents (K, phosphate, myoglobin, CK) into bloodstream. Biggest risk: acute kidney injury from myoglobin pigment nephropathy. Management: AGGRESSIVE IV crystalloid resuscitation (NS or LR, 1-2L bolus then 200-300 mL/hr titrated to urine output >200-300 mL/hr). Monitor urine output, renal function, electrolytes (hyperkalemia → cardiac arrhythmia). Alkalinization with bicarb generally NOT recommended. Treat underlying cause.

cases.hpi: {{patient_name}} presents with acute sore throat, fever >38°C, tonsillar exudates, tender anterior cervical lymphadenopathy, and NO cough. Centor criteria score ≥3: rapid strep test or throat culture indicated. GAS pharyngitis is most common in children 5-15 years. Treatment: penicillin VK PO x 10 days or amoxicillin (first-line). correct_orders: Obtain a thorough history, including feeding habits, weight gain, vomiting, and bowel movements
Physical examination to assess growth parameters, signs of dehydration, abdominal distension, or other relevant findings
Investigations such as complete blood count (CBC), chemistry panel, urinalysis, stool studies, and electrolytes to rule out potential underlying causes like infections, metabolic disorders, or anemia
Consider a swallowing study (videofluoroscopy) or pH monitoring if GERD is suspected

Most commonly triggered by medications: sulfa antibiotics, anti-epileptics (lamotrigine, phenytoin, carbamazepine), allopurinol, NSAIDs, within 1-8 weeks of exposure. This is a medical emergency. cases.hpi: {{patient_name}} presents with unilateral leg swelling, pain, warmth, and erythema. Risk factors: Virchow's triad — stasis (immobilization, long travel), hypercoagulability (malignancy, OCPs, pregnancy, thrombophilia), endothelial injury (surgery, trauma). Exam: Homan's sign unreliable. Measure leg circumference difference. Wells criteria determines pretest probability. If low probability → D-dimer. If D-dimer elevated or high probability → compression ultrasound (proximal DVT). Treatment: most DVT → anticoagulation with DOAC (rivaroxaban, apixaban) or LMWH bridge to warfarin. Duration: provoked = 3 months, unprovoked = 6-12 months or indefinite. NO routine thrombectomy or IVC filter unless anticoagulation contraindicated. Compression stockings for symptom relief and post-thrombotic syndrome prevention.

cases.chief_complaint: Acute chest pain — evaluate for STEMI
cases.case_summary:
Differential: Acute Aortic Dissection, Pulmonary embolism, Pericardial tamponade, Esophageal rupture.

The patient has an ST-elevated inferior myocardial infarction (STEMI). ST elevations will be present in leads II, III, and aVF. The patient should immediately be started on dual antiplatelet therapy (DAPT): Aspirin plus a P2Y12 inhibitor (Ticagrelor is preferred; Clopidogrel is also accepted). A beta blocker and atorvastatin should also be initiated. Cardiology should be consulted and percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) — angioplasty with stent placement — should be performed, as this is the preferred reperfusion strategy.

In the USMLE, immediate PCI is available, so fibrinolytic therapy is not required. If fibrinolysis is ordered, partial credit will be awarded, but full credit requires PCI as the preferred approach. Ticagrelor and Prasugrel are the preferred P2Y12 agents; Clopidogrel is acceptable for full credit. Heparin is optional in STEMI going to cath lab.

cases.hpi: {{patient_name}} presents with chest pain, hypotension, clear lung fields, elevated JVP, and Kussmaul's sign. ECG shows ST elevation in inferior leads (II, III, aVF) with ST elevation in V1 > V3 and ST elevation in V4R (right-sided leads) — indicating RV involvement. RV infarction occurs in ~30% of inferior MIs (usually RCA occlusion). RV is preload-dependent — nitroglycerin and morphine can cause dangerous hypotension because they reduce preload. Treatment: AVOID nitrates and diuretics (reduce preload → worsen RV output). Give IV fluids aggressively to maintain RV preload. Aspirin, P2Y12 inhibitor, anticoagulation. REPERFUSION: emergent PCI (preferred) or fibrinolysis. If hypotensive despite fluids: dobutamine (inotrope). Atropine for bradycardia. Admit to CCU.

cases.hpi: {{patient_name}} presents with sudden onset petechiae, purpura, epistaxis, gum bleeding, and possibly mucosal bleeding in an otherwise well-appearing child. No lymphadenopathy, no hepatosplenomegaly, no fever, no bone pain — distinguishes from leukemia. ITP is an autoimmune destruction of platelets (antibodies against GPIIb/IIIa). Often preceded by viral URI or vaccination 1-4 weeks prior. Labs: ISOLATED thrombocytopenia (platelets <100K, often <20K). Normal Hb, normal WBC, normal peripheral smear (except low platelets). Bone marrow biopsy NOT needed in typical childhood ITP. Treatment: most children (>80%) recover spontaneously within 6 months. If platelets >20K and no bleeding → observation only. If <10K or significant bleeding → prednisone 2-4 mg/kg/day or IVIG or anti-D (if Rh+). Avoid IM injections, contact sports, NSAIDs/aspirin.

cases.hpi: {{patient_name}} presents with high fever, cough (initially dry then productive), dyspnea, pleuritic chest pain, and extrapulmonary symptoms: GI (nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, abdominal pain), hyponatremia (classic lab finding), confusion/AMS, relative bradycardia. History: exposure to contaminated water sources (hot tubs, cooling towers, hotel, cruise ship). Legionella is an atypical pneumonia — intracellular pathogen not seen on Gram stain. Diagnosis: urinary antigen test (detects L. pneumophila serogroup 1 — most common, rapid), sputum culture on specialized media (BCYE agar), PCR. Severe cases require hospitalization. Treatment: macrolides (azithromycin) or respiratory fluoroquinolones (levofloxacin, moxifloxacin). Doxycycline as alternative. Treatment duration 7-14 days (longer if immunocompromised). Report to public health (Legionnaires disease is reportable).

cases.title: Back Pain
cases.hpi: {{patient_name}} presents with chronic low back pain (>3 months), morning stiffness (>30 min) that IMPROVES with exercise and WORSENS with rest. Inflammatory back pain pattern (vs mechanical — worsens with activity). Associated: sacroiliitis, limited spinal mobility (Schober test), enthesitis, peripheral arthritis, uveitis. Young male predominance. Strong association with HLA-B27. Diagnosis: X-ray/MRI of SI joints — sacroiliitis (bamboo spine in advanced disease). Elevated ESR/CRP. Treatment: NSAIDs first-line (excellent response — diagnostic feature). Physical therapy — maintain posture and mobility. If NSAIDs insufficient → TNF inhibitors (infliximab, adalimumab, etanercept). IL-17 inhibitors (secukinumab) also effective. Do NOT recommend bed rest — makes it worse. Exercise program essential.

cases.title: Muscle Weakness
cases.diagnosis: Hyperkalemic Emergency secondary to ACE Inhibitor + NSAID

rationale.ECG: Peaked T, loss of P, wide QRS = severe hyperK.

cases.hpi: {{patient_name}} presents with progressive muscle weakness, fatigue, and palpitations. ECG shows peaked T waves, loss of P waves, widened QRS. Labs reveal severe hyperkalemia (K+ >6.5). Medication history: on ACE inhibitor for HTN and recently started NSAIDs for joint pain. ACEI reduces aldosterone → decreased renal K+ excretion. NSAIDs reduce renal blood flow → further decrease K+ excretion. Combined → dangerous hyperkalemia. Management: IMMEDIATE cardiac membrane stabilization — IV calcium gluconate or calcium chloride (does NOT lower K+, PROTECTS the heart). Then shift K+ intracellularly: IV regular insulin + glucose, beta-agonist (albuterol nebulized), sodium bicarbonate if acidotic. Then eliminate K+: furosemide (if renal function adequate), sodium polystyrene sulfonate (Kayexalate), patiromer, or hemodialysis if refractory. Discontinue ACEI and NSAIDs.

cases.hpi: {{patient_name}} presents with progressive dyspnea, dry cough, fatigue, and bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy on CXR. May have erythema nodosum (painful red nodules on shins), uveitis, parotid enlargement, lupus pernio (purplish facial plaques). Sarcoidosis is a multisystem granulomatous disease of unknown etiology — more common in African Americans. Non-caseating granulomas are the pathologic hallmark. CXR staging: I (BHL only), II (BHL + parenchymal infiltrates), III (parenchymal only), IV (fibrosis). Labs: elevated ACE level (supports but not diagnostic), hypercalcemia/hypercalciuria (increased 1,25-vitamin D from activated macrophages in granulomas). Diagnosis: biopsy showing non-caseating granulomas + exclusion of other causes (TB, fungal, berylliosis). PFTs: restrictive pattern. Treatment: many resolve spontaneously (stage I). If symptomatic or progressive → corticosteroids (prednisone 0.5 mg/kg/day). Methotrexate or azathioprine for steroid-sparing. Anti-TNF for refractory. Monitor for TB reactivation before immunosuppression.

rationale.Refer rheumatology: Early aggressive treatment prevents joint damage.

cases.hpi: {{patient_name}} presents with symmetric polyarthritis involving small joints of hands (MCP, PIP), wrists, and ankles. Morning stiffness >1 hour. Joints are warm, swollen, tender. RA is a chronic autoimmune inflammatory arthritis. Key features: symmetric, polyarticular, involves hands/feet, spares DIP joints (distinguishes from osteoarthritis which involves DIP/PIP, Heberden/Bouchard nodes). Extra-articular: rheumatoid nodules, interstitial lung disease, pericarditis, vasculitis, Felty's syndrome. Labs: RF (rheumatoid factor — 80% sensitive), anti-CCP (anti-citrullinated peptide — very specific >95%), elevated ESR/CRP. X-ray: periarticular osteopenia, joint space narrowing, marginal erosions. Treatment: early aggressive DMARDs — methotrexate first-line. Plus short-term prednisone bridge. If MTX inadequate → add biologic (TNF inhibitor — etanercept, adalimumab). Refer to rheumatology. Physical and occupational therapy.

rationale.Dialysis (if AEIOU indications): AEIOU: Acidosis, Electrolytes, Intoxication, Overload, Uremia.

cases.hpi: {{patient_name}} presents with progressive fatigue, weakness, anorexia, nausea, pruritus, edema, and oliguria. Labs: markedly elevated BUN/Cr, hyperkalemia, metabolic acidosis, anemia (low EPO), hypocalcemia, hyperphosphatemia, secondary hyperparathyroidism. ESRD is irreversible loss of renal function (GFR <15). Most common causes: diabetes, hypertension, glomerulonephritis. Management: renal replacement therapy — hemodialysis, peritoneal dialysis, or kidney transplant. Urgent indications for dialysis: AEIOU — Acidosis, Electrolytes (hyperkalemia), Intoxication (toxins), Overload (volume), Uremia (pericarditis, encephalopathy). cases.title: Headache
cases.hpi: {{patient_name}} presents with chronic daily headache (worse in morning, with Valsalva), transient visual obscurations, pulsatile tinnitus, and diplopia (CN VI palsy from increased ICP). Fundoscopy: bilateral papilledema. IIH is elevated ICP without mass lesion or hydrocephalus, typically in obese women of childbearing age. Risk factors: obesity, recent weight gain, vitamin A excess, tetracyclines, OCPs, steroids. Diagnosis: MRI/MRV brain (normal — rules out mass, venous sinus thrombosis). LP: elevated opening pressure (>25 cm H2O) with normal CSF composition. Treatment: weight loss (most important), acetazolamide (carbonic anhydrase inhibitor — reduces CSF production). Serial ophthalmology: visual fields, optic nerve exam. If vision threatened: optic nerve sheath fenestration or CSF shunting (VP or LP shunt). Discontinue causative medications.

rationale.Acute: stop protein + glucose + insulin: Anabolic state. Dialysis if severe hyperleucinemia.

cases.hpi: {{patient_name}} is a neonate presenting with seizures, poor feeding, vomiting, lethargy, and urine/cerumen that smells like maple syrup (burnt sugar). MSUD is an autosomal recessive inborn error of metabolism — deficiency of branched-chain alpha-ketoacid dehydrogenase complex → accumulation of branched-chain amino acids (leucine, isoleucine, valine) and their ketoacids. Leucine is neurotoxic → encephalopathy, seizures. Newborn screening detects elevated leucine. Diagnosis: plasma amino acids — markedly elevated leucine, isoleucine, valine. Urine organic acids: branched-chain ketoacids. During acute decompensation: remove leucine (dialysis if severe), provide calories (glucose + insulin to promote anabolism), correct electrolyte abnormalities. Long-term: dietary restriction of BCAAs with special formula, liver transplant for severe cases.

cases.hpi: {{patient_name}} presents found unconscious with cherry-red skin, bitter almond breath odor (only 40% can detect), high anion gap metabolic acidosis, and elevated lactate. Cyanide inhibits cytochrome c oxidase (Complex IV of ETC) → blocks oxidative phosphorylation → cells cannot use oxygen → tissue hypoxia despite normal PaO2 → anaerobic metabolism → lactic acidosis. Sources: smoke inhalation (burning plastics/wool), industrial exposure, sodium nitroprusside infusion. Treatment: hydroxocobalamin (Cyanokit — first-line, binds cyanide to form cyanocobalamin which is renally excreted). rationale.High-dose Aspirin / NSAIDs: 650mg aspirin q4-6h. Avoid steroids if possible.

cases.hpi: {{patient_name}} presents with pleuritic chest pain, fever, malaise, and pericardial friction rub 2-6 weeks after a myocardial infarction. Dressler syndrome is an autoimmune-mediated pericarditis occurring post-MI (or post-cardiac surgery) — immune response to exposed myocardial antigens. ECG: diffuse ST elevation, PR depression (pericarditis pattern). Echo: pericardial effusion (usually small). Differentiate from peri-infarct pericarditis (occurs within days of MI, localized ECG changes over infarct zone, more directly due to transmural necrosis). Treatment: high-dose aspirin (650mg q4-6h) or NSAIDs (ibuprofen). Colchicine added for symptom reduction and recurrence prevention. Avoid steroids unless refractory (impair myocardial healing). NOT heparin (risk of hemorrhagic pericardial effusion/tamponade).

cases.title: Chronic Diarrhea
cases.hpi: {{patient_name}} presents with severe, refractory peptic ulcer disease, chronic watery diarrhea, abdominal pain, and GI bleeding. Multiple ulcers in atypical locations (distal duodenum, jejunum). ZES is caused by a gastrin-secreting neuroendocrine tumor (gastrinoma) — most commonly in the duodenum or pancreas → massive gastric acid hypersecretion → severe PUD and diarrhea (acid inactivates pancreatic enzymes + damages mucosa). Often associated with MEN1. Diagnosis: fasting serum gastrin level — markedly elevated (>1000 pg/mL or >10x normal). If borderline → secretin stimulation test (paradoxical increase in gastrin in ZES). Localize tumor: somatostatin receptor scintigraphy (Octreoscan), CT/MRI, EUS. Treatment: high-dose PPI (omeprazole, pantoprazole) to control acid hypersecretion. Surgical resection if localized. If metastatic or unresectable → long-term PPI + octreotide.

cases.hpi: {{patient_name}} presents with persistent back pain (pathologic vertebral compression fractures), fatigue (normocytic anemia), and possibly hypercalcemia. Multiple myeloma is a malignant proliferation of plasma cells in bone marrow → monoclonal immunoglobulin (M protein) production. Classic CRAB criteria: hyperCalcemia, Renal insufficiency, Anemia, Bone lesions (lytic lesions on X-ray/skeletal survey). Labs: elevated total protein with globulin gap, M spike on SPEP, immunofixation confirms monoclonal Ig (IgG most common), elevated kappa/lambda free light chains with abnormal ratio, Bence Jones protein in urine (UPEP). Bone marrow biopsy: >10% clonal plasma cells. Skeletal survey: lytic punched-out lesions. Treatment: induction (bortezomib + lenalidomide + dexamethasone), +/- autologous stem cell transplant if eligible. Bisphosphonates (zoledronic acid) for bone disease.

cases.hpi: {{patient_name}} presents found unconscious in an enclosed space with possible exposure (car exhaust, faulty heater, fire). Cherry-red skin, headache, confusion, nausea. cases.hpi: {{patient_name}} presents with fragile skin, blistering lesions on sun-exposed areas (hands, face, forearms), milia, hyperpigmentation, and hypertrichosis. PCT is the most common porphyria — caused by deficiency of uroporphyrinogen decarboxylase (UROD) → accumulation of uroporphyrins in skin → photosensitivity. Acquired form associated with: alcohol, hepatitis C, HIV, hemochromatosis, estrogen therapy. Diagnosis: elevated uroporphyrins and heptacarboxyl porphyrins in urine, plasma porphyrins (peak at 620nm), stool isocoproporphyrin. Treatment: phlebotomy (remove iron — goal ferritin low-normal) or low-dose hydroxychloroquine (mobilizes porphyrins). Avoid sun exposure, alcohol, and estrogens. Screen for HCV, HIV, hemochromatosis.

cases.title: Vaginal Discharge
cases.hpi: {{patient_name}} presents with profuse, frothy, yellow-green malodorous vaginal discharge, vulvar irritation, dysuria, and dyspareunia. Exam reveals strawberry cervix (punctate hemorrhages) and vaginal erythema. Caused by Trichomonas vaginalis — flagellated protozoan. Diagnosis: wet mount shows motile trichomonads (flagellated organisms). Vaginal pH >4.5. Whiff test may be positive. NAAT (PCR) is gold standard — more sensitive than wet mount. cases.title: Fatigue
cases.hpi: {{patient_name}} presents with excessive daytime sleepiness, loud snoring, witnessed apneas, morning headaches, and fatigue. Risk factors: obesity, large neck circumference, male, retrognathia. OSA = repetitive upper airway collapse during sleep → apnea/hypopnea → oxygen desaturation → sympathetic surge → disrupted sleep. STOP-BANG screening questionnaire. Complications: hypertension, atrial fibrillation, pulmonary hypertension, cor pulmonale, metabolic syndrome, motor vehicle accidents. Diagnosis: polysomnography (sleep study) — AHI (apnea-hypopnea index) >5 = OSA. Mild 5-15, moderate 15-30, severe >30. Treatment: CPAP (first-line for moderate-severe). Weight loss (most important lifestyle). Oral appliance for mild-mod. Positional therapy. Surgical (UPPP) if CPAP intolerant.

rationale.Ca / PTH / PTHrP: High Ca, low PTH, elevated PTHrP = malignancy.

cases.hpi: {{patient_name}} presents with progressive somnolence, confusion, fatigue, constipation, polyuria, polydipsia, and nausea. Labs: elevated calcium (>11), low PTH (rules out primary hyperparathyroidism), elevated PTHrP. Hypercalcemia of malignancy is the most common cause of hypercalcemia in hospitalized patients. Mechanisms: PTHrP secretion (squamous cell cancers — lung, head/neck), osteolytic bone metastases (breast, multiple myeloma), excess 1,25-vitamin D (lymphoma). Treatment: aggressive IV normal saline (3-4L/day) to promote calciuresis. Then IV bisphosphonates (zoledronic acid or pamidronate — inhibit osteoclast activity). Calcitonin for rapid short-term reduction. Denosumab if refractory. Treat underlying malignancy. Monitor for arrhythmias (shortened QT on ECG).

cases.hpi: {{patient_name}} presents with recurrent falls, dizziness, lightheadedness, and near-syncope upon standing (within 3 min of standing). Orthostatic hypotension = drop in SBP ≥20mmHg or DBP ≥10mmHg within 3 min of standing. Causes: medications (antihypertensives — especially alpha-blockers, diuretics, nitrates, TCAs, dopaminergics), hypovolemia, autonomic neuropathy (DM, Parkinson's), prolonged bed rest. Workup: orthostatic vital signs, medication review, CBC (anemia), BMP (dehydration, electrolyte), EKG, consider autonomic testing. Treatment: review and adjust medications. Non-pharmacologic: increase fluid/salt intake (if no CHF), compression stockings, elevate head of bed, slow position changes, avoid prolonged standing. If needed: fludrocortisone (mineralocorticoid — expand volume) or midodrine (alpha-1 agonist).

cases.chief_complaint: Hematemesis and melena in a patient with alcoholic cirrhosis
cases.case_summary:
Differential: Esophageal varices, peptic ulcer disease, Mallory-Weiss tear, gastric erosions, malignancy.

Esophageal varices are dilated submucosal veins that develop as a consequence of portal hypertension, most commonly from cirrhosis. This case presents a classic scenario: a 55-year-old man with alcoholic cirrhosis presenting with hematemesis and melena, found to have severe anemia (Hct 24%, Hgb 8.0), mild coagulopathy (INR 1.8), and thrombocytopenia (platelets 100,000).

The definitive diagnosis is made via urgent esophagogastroduodenoscopy (EGD) with band ligation. Acute management: type and crossmatch, cautious IV resuscitation, restrictive PRBC transfusion (Hb 7–9 g/dL), octreotide IV, IV PPI, ceftriaxone prophylaxis in cirrhotics with GI bleed, and NPO for endoscopy. With platelets 100,000 and INR 1.8, platelet or FFP transfusion is NOT required. Spironolactone is contraindicated during acute variceal hemorrhage. After stabilization: non-selective beta-blocker for secondary prophylaxis, hepatitis A/B vaccination, alcohol cessation counseling, and lactulose to prevent hepatic encephalopathy.

cases.title: Nocturnal Enuresis
cases.diagnosis: Severe Obstructive Sleep Apnea with Secondary Nocturnal Enuresis
cases.hpi: {{patient_name}} presents with primary or secondary nocturnal enuresis (bedwetting), loud snoring, restless sleep, daytime fatigue, and behavioral issues. Severe OSA causes nocturnal enuresis through: (1) increased intra-abdominal pressure during apnea → increased venous return → ANP/BNP release → increased nocturnal urine production; (2) disrupted sleep architecture → decreased arousal to bladder distention. Polysomnography confirms severe OSA (AHI >30). Treatment: CPAP or adenotonsillectomy if large tonsils/adenoids. Treating the OSA often resolves the enuresis. Do NOT treat enuresis in isolation without evaluating for sleep-disordered breathing.
